title: Customer Experience (CX) Professional
tagline: Design, deliver and measure experiences that Pakistani customers remember for the right reasons, and build the culture that keeps them coming back.
description:
Customers in Pakistan now compare your branch, your helpline and your app with the best experience they have had anywhere. This certification teaches the full CX discipline in practical terms.

- **Why experience matters:** the difference between customer service and customer experience, the economics of loyalty, moments of truth and the role of emotion.
- **Understanding customers:** voice of the customer, personas, journey maps, pain points and service blueprints.
- **Delivering excellence:** empathetic communication in Urdu and English, handling complaints and difficult customers, service recovery and consistent omnichannel service across branch, call centre, WhatsApp and app.
- **Measuring what matters:** calculating and interpreting NPS, CSAT, CES and first-contact resolution, closing the loop and avoiding metric gaming.
- **Leading a CX culture:** service standards, employee experience, empowerment, complaint management in regulated sectors, continuous improvement and building the business case.

Every session uses realistic Pakistani scenarios and ends with a scored test. The final exam is demanding and includes calculations, so plan to practise.
audience: Frontline staff in branches, stores, hotels and contact centres who deal with customers every day
Back-office and operations staff whose processes shape what customers experience
Team leads and supervisors responsible for service quality and complaint handling
CX, service quality and complaint-management managers in banks, telecoms, insurers and retailers
Professionals preparing to move into a customer experience or quality role
outcomes: Explain the difference between customer service and customer experience and estimate the financial value of loyalty
Map a customer journey and a service blueprint to locate pain points and their root causes
Handle complaints and difficult customers with a structured, empathetic recovery approach across channels
Calculate and correctly interpret NPS, CSAT, CES and first-contact resolution, and spot gamed metrics
Design a closed-loop feedback process that fixes both individual cases and underlying causes
Describe how complaints are handled and escalated in regulated sectors such as banking and insurance
Build a practical CX improvement plan and business case that leadership will fund

quest.name: The Lanterns of Roshan Nagar
quest.premise: Roshan Nagar is a busy city of customers whose lanterns dim each time a company lets them down. You have been appointed its new Experience Warden. Walk through five districts, from the city gate to the citadel, learning to see the city through its people's eyes, to repair broken promises, to read the true signals of loyalty and to light a culture that keeps every lantern burning.

badge.name: Roshan Nagar Experience Warden
badge.description: Awarded to professionals who proved they can design, deliver, measure and lead customer experience to a demanding standard.

sessions.title: What CX Really Is: Loyalty, Moments of Truth and Emotion
sessions.summary: Learn what separates customer experience from customer service, why loyal customers are worth so much more than new ones, which moments decide how customers feel, and how emotion shapes what they remember.
objectives: Distinguish customer experience from customer service and explain who owns each
Estimate customer lifetime value and show how small retention gains change it
Identify moments of truth in a customer relationship and prioritise them
Explain how emotion, effort and the peak-end effect shape what customers remember

cards.title: Customer service is a department; customer experience is everything
cards.body:
Many organisations say "CX" when they mean the helpline. The two are related but not the same.

**Customer service** is the help a customer receives when they ask for it: the agent who answers the call, the branch officer who fixes a card issue, the store assistant who processes a return. It is mostly reactive and owned by a service team.

**Customer experience (CX)** is the customer's total perception of the organisation, built from every interaction across the whole relationship: the advert that set expectations, the account-opening form, the SMS alerts, the bill, the app update that moved a button, the delivery rider's behaviour and, yes, the helpline. Most of these are designed by people who never speak to a customer: product, IT, operations, finance, legal and marketing.

| | Customer service | Customer experience |
|---|---|---|
| Scope | Assisted interactions | The entire relationship |
| Timing | Mostly after a need or problem | Before, during and after purchase |
| Owner | Service team | Every function, led from the top |
| Typical question | "Did we solve this case?" | "Would this customer choose us again?" |

A useful test: if a customer has to call you, something in the experience may already have failed. A billing statement that customers cannot understand generates calls. Excellent agents can soften that pain, but only a redesigned statement removes it.

This is why CX professionals spend as much time with process owners and data as with frontline staff. Great service is one ingredient of great experience; it cannot compensate indefinitely for a broken product, confusing policies or slow processes behind the counter.

cards.title: The SIM replacement that took three visits
cards.body:
Ayesha Siddiqui in Multan lost her phone and visited a telecom franchise to replace her SIM. The staff member was polite and apologetic, but the biometric device was not working, so she was asked to come back the next day. On the second visit, she was told her CNIC copy was needed even though the biometric check had succeeded. On the third visit the SIM was issued, but her mobile wallet stayed blocked for 48 hours because a separate team had to re-activate it.

In the satisfaction survey after the third visit, Ayesha rated the staff 5 out of 5 for courtesy. She also told her family she was thinking of moving her number to another network.

**What went wrong was not "service".** Each person she met was friendly. The experience failed because:

- Equipment maintenance at franchises was nobody's priority.
- Document requirements were inconsistent and not explained up front.
- The wallet re-activation sat in a different department with its own queue.

The company's service-quality report showed high courtesy scores and concluded all was well. A CX view looks at the whole journey ("replace my lost SIM and get back to normal") and measures how long it takes, how many visits it needs and how the customer feels at the end. That view would have exposed three fixable causes owned by operations, compliance and the wallet team, not by the franchise staff.

cards.question: A bank's call-centre agents score very highly on courtesy, yet complaints about a confusing loan statement keep rising. What is the most accurate CX diagnosis?
options: Agents need more empathy training so that callers feel better about the statement
The statement design is an experience problem that service excellence alone cannot remove
Courtesy scores are unreliable and should be removed from the quality form
The call centre should be given ownership of the statement design
cards.explanation: The root cause sits outside the call centre: the statement creates the need to call. Good agents soften the pain but cannot remove it. More training treats the symptom, and handing statement design to the call centre ignores that CX is shared across functions.

cards.title: The economics of loyalty
cards.body:
CX earns a seat in the boardroom when it is expressed in rupees. The core idea is **customer lifetime value (CLV)**: the profit a customer generates over the whole relationship.

A simple, widely used estimate:

- **Expected relationship length (years) ≈ 1 ÷ annual churn rate**, where churn rate = 1 − retention rate.
- **CLV ≈ average annual profit per customer × expected relationship length.**

If a mobile operator keeps 80% of its customers each year, churn is 20%, so the average customer stays about 1 ÷ 0.20 = 5 years. This simple version ignores discounting and growth in spending, so treat it as a rough guide, not a valuation.

**Why loyalty pays more than the arithmetic suggests:**

- **Acquisition is expensive.** Advertising, sales commissions, SIM subsidies, account-opening costs and KYC checks are all spent before a new customer earns anything.
- **Loyal customers buy more over time**: a second product, a higher package, an upgraded card.
- **They cost less to serve** because they know how things work.
- **They recommend you.** In Pakistan, family and friends strongly influence choices of bank, school, hospital and insurer. One unhappy story told at a family dinner can cost several future customers.
- **They forgive occasional mistakes** if the relationship has been good.

The flip side is that unhappy customers who stay are not truly loyal. Many Pakistani customers keep a salary account at one bank only because their employer chose it, while their savings, car loan and card sit elsewhere. That is **captive** behaviour, not loyalty, and it disappears the moment switching becomes easy. Real loyalty is a mix of behaviour (staying and buying more) and attitude (preferring and recommending).

cards.title: Putting a rupee value on retention
cards.body:
Bilal Ahmed, the new CX lead at a mid-sized bank in Lahore, wants funding to fix the debit-card replacement journey, which is the top reason for complaints among retail customers.

His numbers:

- Average annual profit per retail customer: **PKR 12,000**
- Current retention: **80%**, so churn is 20% and the expected relationship is 1 ÷ 0.20 = **5 years**
- Current CLV ≈ 12,000 × 5 = **PKR 60,000**

If the improvements raise retention to **85%**, churn falls to 15% and the expected relationship becomes 1 ÷ 0.15 ≈ **6.67 years**. CLV rises to about 12,000 × 6.67 ≈ **PKR 80,000**.

A five-point retention improvement adds roughly **PKR 20,000** of value per customer, a 33% increase. Across a base of 200,000 retail customers, that is about **PKR 4 billion** of lifetime value.

Bilal is careful in how he presents this:

- He shows it as an estimate, without discounting, and states his assumptions.
- He does not claim that the card fix alone will deliver five points. He links it to evidence: customers who complained about cards churned at almost twice the average rate in the previous year.
- He proposes a pilot in two regions with a control group, so the effect can be measured rather than assumed.

The leadership team approves the pilot because the logic is clear and the risk is small. Notice that the rupee argument, not the word "delight", opened the door.

cards.title: Common mistake: rewarding new customers and punishing loyal ones
cards.body:
Many companies give their best offers only to new customers: free months, waived fees, higher profit rates. Existing customers see the advert, ask for the same deal and are told it is "for new customers only". The message received is that loyalty is for fools.

Before approving an acquisition campaign, ask: **what will our existing customers think when they see this?** Consider a matching loyalty benefit, or at least a script that offers something meaningful to long-standing customers who ask.

cards.title: Moments of truth
cards.body:
Not every interaction matters equally. A **moment of truth** is a point in the relationship where the customer forms or changes their opinion of you in a way that is hard to reverse. The phrase was popularised by an airline chief executive who argued that each brief contact between staff and passengers decided whether the airline succeeded.

CX practitioners often think of moments of truth at three levels:

- **First impressions**: the first visit to a branch, the onboarding call, the first bill. Customers judge quickly and then look for evidence that confirms the judgement.
- **Moments of need**: when something goes wrong or matters a lot. A fraud alert on a card, a hospital claim under a health policy, a delayed flight, a failed remittance before Eid. Emotions are high and the customer is watching closely.
- **Moments of decision**: renewal of an insurance policy, a contract ending, a competitor's offer. These are where the accumulated experience turns into a stay-or-leave choice.

**How to find them:**

1. Look at where complaints and repeat contacts cluster.
2. Ask customers what they remember, good and bad. Memories point to moments of truth.
3. Look at where churn rises: for example, customers whose first insurance claim was handled badly are far more likely to lapse.
4. Notice where stakes are high: money, health, family, deadlines, public embarrassment.

**Why it matters:** budgets and attention are limited. A bank that polishes its marble floors while its fraud-blocking process leaves customers stranded at a petrol pump has invested in the wrong moment. Identify the handful of moments that drive loyalty and design them deliberately, with clear standards, empowered staff and backup plans.

cards.question: An insurer has budget to redesign only one part of its health-policy journey. Which part is most likely to be a moment of truth?
options: The design of the annual policy renewal letter
The welcome pack sent after the policy is issued
Cashless approval at the hospital desk when a family member is admitted
The colour scheme of the customer portal
cards.explanation: Hospital admission is a moment of need: stakes and emotions are very high and the customer is testing whether the promise is real. A smooth or failed approval there shapes loyalty far more than a welcome pack or renewal letter, which matter but are lower-stakes.

cards.title: Emotion: what customers remember, not what happened
cards.body:
Customers do not keep a spreadsheet of every interaction. They keep **memories**, and memories are shaped by emotion.

**The peak-end effect.** Research in behavioural psychology shows that people judge a past experience largely by its most intense moment (the peak, good or bad) and by how it ended, rather than by its total duration or the average of every minute. A long wait that ends with a warm, competent resolution is often remembered better than a short interaction that ends with a curt "nothing can be done".

Practical implications:

- **Design the ending.** The last minute of a call, the handover of car keys after servicing, the checkout at a hotel. A clear summary, a confirmed next step and a sincere thank you cost almost nothing.
- **Remove the worst peak first.** One humiliating moment, such as being told loudly at a counter that a payment bounced, can outweigh many pleasant ones.
- **Create a positive peak deliberately** where it is cheap: a branch manager who remembers a customer's name, an agent who proactively waives a small fee after a long fault.

**Effort drives negative emotion.** Repeating details, being transferred, filling the same form twice and visiting in person for something that should be digital create frustration, even when the final outcome is correct.

**Emotions are contagious.** A stressed, under-supported agent transmits stress. That is one reason employee experience appears in Session 5.

**Feeling respected matters a great deal in Pakistan's service culture.** Customers notice who is greeted first, whether an elderly person is offered a seat, and whether they are spoken to in a language and tone they are comfortable with. Dignity is part of the product.

cards.title: Two check-outs at a hotel in Murree
cards.body:
Two families stay at the same hotel in Murree over a long weekend. Both experience the same problem: hot water fails on the second morning for about three hours.

**Family A (the Qureshis):** At check-out, the receptionist is busy on the phone and prints the bill without looking up. Mr Qureshi mentions the hot water. The receptionist says, "Sir, it was a general issue, everyone faced it." The family leaves annoyed. Their review mentions "cold water, careless staff" and gives two stars.

**Family B (the Baloch family):** The duty manager, Saima, has the list of affected rooms. At check-out she says, "Mr Baloch, I know the hot water failed on Saturday morning, and with small children that is very difficult. I am sorry. We have removed the breakfast charge for that day, and our engineer replaced the faulty valve so it should not happen again." She also hands the children a small box of local sweets for the road. Their review mentions the cold water too, but says "they owned it and fixed it" and gives four stars.

**Analysis:**

- The failure (the negative peak) was identical.
- The ending was completely different, and it shaped the memory.
- Saima's response used information the hotel already had. The cost was one breakfast and a box of sweets.
- She named the specific impact (small children), took ownership, gave a concrete remedy and explained the permanent fix. Those elements of service recovery are studied in depth in Session 3.

cards.title: A quick way to spot emotional pain points
cards.body: When reviewing complaints or call recordings, highlight the words customers use: **"again", "still", "third time", "nobody", "embarrassed", "helpless", "phir se", "koi sunta nahi"**. These words signal repeated effort, lack of ownership and loss of dignity, the three emotions most strongly linked to customers leaving. Count them by journey to find where emotion runs hottest.

cards.question: Under the peak-end effect, which change is likely to improve how customers remember a 20-minute visit to a passport-style service counter at the lowest cost?
options: Cutting the visit from 20 to 17 minutes by adding one more counter
Repainting the waiting hall in brighter colours
Sending a satisfaction survey the next day
Ending each visit with a clear confirmation of what happens next and when
cards.explanation: The peak-end effect means the ending weighs heavily in memory. A clear, confident close is almost free and improves the remembered experience. A small cut in duration helps but costs more and changes memory less. A survey measures the experience but does not improve it.

cards.title: Take-aways from the Gate of First Impressions
items: Customer service is assisted help; customer experience is the customer's total perception across the whole relationship, shaped by every function.
CLV ≈ annual profit per customer × (1 ÷ churn rate). Small retention gains create large increases in value.
Captive customers who stay because switching is hard are not loyal; real loyalty combines staying, buying more and recommending.
Moments of truth (first impressions, moments of need, moments of decision) deserve most of your design effort.
Customers remember peaks and endings; remove the worst peak first and design the ending deliberately.
Effort, lack of ownership and loss of dignity are the emotions most strongly linked to leaving.

cards.prompt: Think of one journey your customers go through with your organisation. What is its most likely moment of truth, what does the ending currently feel like for the customer, and which department actually controls that moment?

quiz.question: Which statement best captures the difference between customer service and customer experience?
options: Customer service covers digital channels such as apps and chat, while customer experience covers branches and stores
Service is assisted help when asked; experience is the total perception formed across every interaction
Customer experience is the marketing team's name for customer service
Customer service is measured by NPS while customer experience is measured by CSAT
quiz.explanation: Service is the assisted, often reactive help a customer receives; experience is the overall perception formed across the entire relationship, including interactions designed by people who never meet customers. The channel split and metric split are both false distinctions.

quiz.question: A broadband provider earns an average annual profit of PKR 15,000 per customer and retains 75% of customers each year. Using the simple CLV estimate taught in this session, what is the approximate lifetime value of a customer?
quiz.explanation: Churn = 1 − 0.75 = 0.25, so expected relationship ≈ 1 ÷ 0.25 = 4 years. CLV ≈ 15,000 × 4 = PKR 60,000. PKR 11,250 multiplies profit by the retention rate, and PKR 20,000 divides profit by retention instead of churn.

quiz.question: Sana's card is blocked by a fraud alert while she is paying for medicines at a pharmacy in Peshawar late at night. In CX terms, this is best described as:
options: A moment of need, which is a high-stakes moment of truth
A first-impression moment that has little effect once the relationship is established
A moment of decision, because she must decide whether to pay in cash
A routine transaction that is unlikely to shape her view of the bank
quiz.explanation: A blocked card during an urgent purchase is a moment of need: emotions and stakes are high, and the bank's response will strongly shape her opinion. It is not a first impression, and a moment of decision refers to stay-or-leave points such as renewals or competitor offers.

quiz.question: A clinic's patients wait about 40 minutes, which is long, but surveys show that patients who were seen by Dr Farah rate the visit far higher than patients of other doctors with similar waits. Dr Farah ends every consultation by summarising the plan and asking if the patient has any worries. Which idea best explains the difference?
options: Patients rate shorter consultations more highly
Total waiting time is the main driver of how patients remember a clinic visit
The ending of an experience weighs heavily in how it is remembered
Patients cannot judge medical quality, so they rate randomly
quiz.explanation: Waits were similar, so duration does not explain the gap. The peak-end effect does: Dr Farah's clear, caring close shapes the memory of the whole visit. Nothing in the scenario suggests shorter consultations or random ratings.

quiz.question: A telecom operator keeps 90% of its subscribers each year. Management proposes a programme expected to raise retention to 92%. Using expected relationship length ≈ 1 ÷ churn, how does the average customer's expected relationship change?
options: From 9 years to about 11 years
From 10 years to 12.5 years
From 10 years to about 10.2 years
From 1.1 years to about 1.09 years
quiz.explanation: Churn falls from 10% to 8%. 1 ÷ 0.10 = 10 years and 1 ÷ 0.08 = 12.5 years, a 25% increase from just two points of retention. Option C wrongly scales by the retention change; option D divides by retention instead of churn.

quiz.question: Most salary-account holders at a bank keep their savings and car financing with competitors but rarely close the salary account because their employer pays through it. How should the CX team describe these customers?
options: Captive rather than loyal: they stay because switching is hard
Highly loyal, because a high retention rate is the best evidence of loyalty
Detractors, because they use competitors for other products
Advocates, because they have kept the account for years
quiz.explanation: Retention alone does not prove loyalty. These customers stay because the employer chose the bank, while their preference is shown by moving other business elsewhere. Calling them detractors assumes a survey score we do not have; calling them advocates assumes recommendation.

quiz.question: Which of these is the strongest reason why designing the end of an interaction is a cost-effective CX lever?
options: Customers usually forget the beginning of interactions entirely
Regulators only review the final step of a customer journey
Endings are the only part of a journey the company controls
Endings carry heavy weight in memory and can often be improved with little cost
quiz.explanation: The peak-end effect gives endings disproportionate influence on memory, and a clear summary, confirmed next step or small gesture is cheap. Customers do not forget beginnings entirely, and companies control far more than endings.

quiz.question: A retailer launches a campaign offering new loyalty-card holders 20% off for three months. Long-standing customers who ask for the same offer are told it is for new members only. What is the main CX risk?
options: The campaign will be so successful that stores become overcrowded and service quality drops for everyone
New customers will not understand the terms
Existing customers learn that loyalty is not valued, weakening retention of the base
The discount will reduce the CSAT score of new customers
quiz.explanation: Rewarding only new customers signals to existing ones that their loyalty earns nothing, which can push them to switch and undercuts the more profitable base. The other options are minor or unrelated to the core risk.

quiz.question: During a review of complaint transcripts, which group of customer phrases is the strongest warning sign of churn risk?
options: "Third time I am calling", "nobody takes ownership", "I felt embarrassed"
"Please send me the full details by email", "what are your branch timings on Saturday?"
"Is there a discount on this package", "can I upgrade"
"Thank you for your help", "I will wait for the SMS"
quiz.explanation: Repeated effort, lack of ownership and loss of dignity are the emotional signals most strongly linked to leaving. The other groups are routine requests, buying signals or positive signals.

quiz.question: A CX lead estimates that improving retention from 80% to 85% raises CLV from PKR 60,000 to about PKR 80,000. The finance head asks why the case should be trusted. Which response best strengthens the case?
options: Increase the assumed retention gain to ten points so the numbers look more convincing
State the assumptions, link the fix to churn evidence and propose a pilot with a control group
Remove the numbers and present customer quotes and complaint stories instead, since CX is about emotion
Argue that every leading company invests in CX, so the bank must too
quiz.explanation: Credible CX cases show assumptions, connect the proposed fix to observed behaviour, and test the effect with a pilot and control group. Inflating assumptions damages credibility; quotes and benchmarks support a case but do not replace evidence.

sessions.title: Understanding Customers: Voice, Personas, Journeys and Blueprints
sessions.summary: Learn to listen to customers systematically, build personas based on real needs, map journeys from the customer's point of view, trace pain points to root causes and use service blueprints to see what happens behind the counter.
objectives: Design a voice-of-the-customer programme that combines solicited, unsolicited and operational data
Build needs-based personas that avoid stereotypes
Map a current-state customer journey and identify pain points and opportunities
Use root-cause tools and service blueprints to locate where and why journeys fail

cards.title: Voice of the customer: three ways to listen
cards.body:
A **voice-of-the-customer (VoC)** programme is the organised way a company collects, analyses and acts on what customers say and do. Good programmes combine three kinds of input:

**1. Solicited feedback**: what you ask for. Surveys after a transaction, periodic relationship surveys, interviews, focus groups and customer panels.
- *Transactional* surveys follow a specific interaction (a call, a delivery, a claim) and help fix processes.
- *Relationship* surveys measure overall perception at regular intervals and help track loyalty.

**2. Unsolicited feedback**: what customers say without being asked. Complaints, compliments, social media posts, app-store reviews, WhatsApp messages, comments made to branch staff, and call recordings. It is often more honest and more emotional than survey answers.

**3. Operational (behavioural) data**: what customers actually do. Repeat calls, abandoned app journeys, dormant accounts, policy lapses, returns, time spent in queues. Behaviour often reveals problems customers never report.

**Making it work in Pakistan:**

- Offer surveys and complaint channels in **Urdu as well as English**, and in regional languages where your customer base needs it. Many customers will not complain in English.
- Remember that many customers are reluctant to criticise staff face to face, out of politeness or to avoid conflict. Low complaint volume does not mean high satisfaction.
- Do not ignore **frontline staff**. Tellers, riders and agents hear the same frustrations every day. A simple weekly "what did customers struggle with?" channel is a cheap, rich VoC source.
- Text analytics on call notes and chats can help, but someone must read real verbatims regularly. Numbers tell you where; words tell you why.

The test of a VoC programme is not how much data it collects but how many changes it causes.

cards.title: Survey questions that mislead you
cards.body:
Watch for these common faults:

- **Leading questions:** "How satisfied were you with our quick service?" assumes it was quick.
- **Double-barrelled questions:** "Was the agent polite and knowledgeable?" Which one are they rating?
- **Too long:** completion collapses after a few questions on a phone screen.
- **Poor translation:** a literal Urdu translation of an English scale can change its meaning. Test with real customers.
- **Wrong timing:** surveying a claim before it is paid measures hope, not experience.

cards.question: A telecom company's complaint volumes are low, but monthly data shows that many prepaid customers stop recharging after their first two months. What does this pattern most suggest?
options: Prepaid customers are satisfied, as shown by low complaints
The company should stop measuring complaints
Operational data is revealing a problem that customers are not reporting through complaints
The pattern is normal and needs no investigation
cards.explanation: Behavioural data (stopping recharges) shows customers leaving silently. Low complaints do not mean satisfaction, especially where customers avoid confrontation. Complaints remain useful, so stopping their measurement would be wrong.

cards.title: Personas built on needs, not stereotypes
cards.body:
A **persona** is a short, realistic profile of a customer group that shares similar goals, needs and behaviours. It helps teams design for real people instead of an imaginary "average customer".

**A useful persona includes:**

- A name and short context (to make it memorable, not to define the group)
- **Goals**: what they are trying to achieve
- **Needs and expectations** from you
- **Behaviours**: channels used, digital comfort, who helps them decide
- **Frustrations and fears**
- A quote in their own words, drawn from research

**Build personas from evidence.** Interviews, observation, survey data and behavioural data should show that the group is real and sizeable. A persona invented in a meeting room usually reflects the team's assumptions.

**Segment by need, not only demographics.** Two customers of the same age and income may behave very differently. A 55-year-old shopkeeper in Faisalabad who runs his business on a mobile wallet may be more digital than a 30-year-old office worker who prefers to visit the branch. Needs-based personas, such as "the time-poor professional", "the cautious first-time saver" or "the remittance-dependent family", lead to better design decisions than "males 25–34".

**Avoid stereotypes.** Do not assume that women, older customers or rural customers cannot use digital channels, or that a particular community prefers a particular product. Let data speak.

**Keep the number small.** Three to six personas is usually enough. Too many and nobody remembers them; too few and important differences disappear.

Personas earn their keep when they are used: in design reviews ("would Nasreen be able to do this on her phone?"), in prioritisation and in training.

cards.title: Persona: Nasreen, the remittance-dependent household manager
cards.body:
A bank's research with recipients of home remittances in central Punjab produced this persona.

**Nasreen, 42, Sialkot district.** Manages the household budget; her husband works in the Gulf and sends money every month.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Goals** | Receive money on time, especially before school fees and Eid; keep the family's finances private |
| **Needs** | Certainty about when money will arrive; a simple way to collect it; help in Urdu or Punjabi |
| **Behaviours** | Uses WhatsApp daily; is cautious with banking apps; relies on her son to set things up; visits the branch when unsure |
| **Frustrations** | "The money is sent but nobody can tell me where it is." Being asked for documents she did not bring; long queues on the first days of the month |
| **Fears** | Fraud calls pretending to be the bank; making a mistake in the app and losing money |

**Design implications the team drew:**

- Send a proactive SMS and WhatsApp-style notification in Urdu when a remittance arrives, with the amount and collection options.
- Publish a short, printed checklist of documents at the branch and on WhatsApp.
- Add a fraud-awareness message from a trusted, recognisable source, explaining what the bank will never ask.
- Train branch staff to help customers like Nasreen set up the app step by step, rather than doing it for them.

The persona was based on 18 interviews and transaction data showing that over a third of remittance recipients fitted this pattern.

cards.title: Customer journey mapping
cards.body:
A **customer journey map** shows, from the customer's point of view, the steps they go through to achieve a goal, such as "get a car financed", "switch my mobile package" or "get my insurance claim paid".

**Typical layers of a map:**

1. **Stages**: for example Discover → Apply → Wait → Receive → Use.
2. **Customer actions**: what they do at each stage.
3. **Touchpoints and channels**: website, branch, call centre, WhatsApp, app, agent, SMS.
4. **Thoughts and feelings**: often drawn as an emotion curve rising and falling.
5. **Pain points**: where effort, delay, confusion or anxiety occur.
6. **Opportunities**: ideas to remove pain or create positive moments.

**Principles that separate useful maps from posters:**

- **Start with the customer's goal**, not your internal process. Customers do not care that the credit team and the operations team are separate.
- **Map the current state first**, honestly, before designing the future state.
- **Use evidence**: interviews, call data, complaint data, time measurements, mystery shopping. Mark which points are verified and which are assumptions.
- **Pick one persona per map.** A first-time borrower and an existing premium customer may experience the same process very differently.
- **Include the waits.** The time between touchpoints, when the customer hears nothing, is often where anxiety builds.
- **Involve cross-functional teams**, including people who do the work.

A map is a means, not an end. Finish with a short list of prioritised pain points, their owners and agreed actions. Otherwise the map ends up framed on a wall and nothing changes.

cards.title: Mapping a car financing journey
cards.body:
A bank in Karachi mapped the car financing journey for salaried first-time borrowers. The team interviewed 15 recent customers, pulled application timestamps and listened to 40 calls.

| Stage | Customer action | Feeling | Main pain point |
|---|---|---|---|
| Explore | Uses online calculator, calls helpline | Hopeful | Calculator ignores insurance and processing fees, so the real monthly figure is a surprise |
| Apply | Submits documents at branch | Neutral | Asked for salary slips again after already uploading them |
| Wait | Waits for approval | Anxious | No updates for 9 working days on average; calls the branch repeatedly |
| Approve | Receives approval call | Relieved | Approval letter in technical English, unclear on next steps |
| Delivery | Waits for dealer to release car | Frustrated | Bank and dealer blame each other for delay |

**What the map revealed:**

- The deepest emotional dip was the **wait stage**, where nothing visibly happened. Repeat calls from anxious customers made up a large share of branch phone traffic.
- The fee surprise at the start damaged trust before the journey had really begun.
- No one owned the handover between bank and dealer.

**Actions agreed:**

1. Proactive SMS updates at three milestones during the wait (owner: digital team).
2. An all-in monthly estimate in the calculator (owner: product).
3. A named relationship contact for dealer handovers (owner: auto finance operations).

The team's key insight was that the approval time itself was less painful than the silence during it.

cards.question: A team builds a journey map entirely in a workshop, using what managers believe customers experience. What is the biggest weakness of this map?
options: It probably has too many stages
It reflects internal assumptions rather than evidence from real customers
It does not include the company's organisation chart
It was not created by the marketing department
cards.explanation: Maps must be grounded in evidence such as interviews, data and observation. Managers' beliefs often miss the waits, workarounds and emotions customers actually experience. The number of stages and which department leads are secondary.

cards.title: From pain point to root cause
cards.body:
A **pain point** is what the customer feels: delay, confusion, repetition, anxiety. A **root cause** is why it happens. Fixing symptoms is tempting and usually temporary.

**Three practical tools:**

**1. Pareto analysis.** Sort complaint or contact reasons by volume. In many organisations a small number of causes generates a large share of contacts. Start there.

**2. The five whys.** Ask "why?" repeatedly until you reach something the organisation can change.
- Customers call to ask about their cheque book. *Why?* They do not know when it will arrive. *Why?* There is no status update. *Why?* The courier system does not share tracking with the bank. *Why?* The contract never required it. The fix is in the courier contract, not the call script.

**3. Cause-and-effect (fishbone) diagram.** Group possible causes under headings such as People, Process, Policy, Technology, Partners and Environment. It prevents teams from jumping to blame individuals.

**Signals that you have reached a real root cause:**

- Fixing it would prevent the problem for many customers, not just one.
- It is within someone's control and has a clear owner.
- It explains the pattern in the data (for example, why the problem is worse in some branches or months).

**Beware "staff attitude" as a root cause.** It is sometimes true, but often staff behaviour is a symptom of targets, tools, training or workload. Ask why the attitude occurs before deciding the answer is more training.

cards.title: Service blueprints: seeing behind the counter
cards.body:
A journey map shows what the customer experiences. A **service blueprint** adds what the organisation does to deliver it, so you can see where failures originate.

**Layers of a blueprint (top to bottom):**

1. **Physical evidence**: what the customer sees or receives (form, SMS, app screen, receipt, branch signage).
2. **Customer actions**: the steps the customer takes.
3. **Frontstage actions**: what staff or systems do in view of the customer (teller, agent, app).
4. **Line of visibility**: everything below this line is invisible to the customer.
5. **Backstage actions**: staff actions the customer does not see (verification, approvals, data entry).
6. **Support processes**: systems, policies, partners and other departments that enable the service (core banking, courier, credit bureau checks, IT).

**What to look for:**

- **Fail points**: steps where errors are likely, such as manual data re-entry.
- **Wait points**: queues and handovers where the customer is left waiting.
- **Too many handovers** between teams, each with its own queue.
- **Frontstage promises that backstage cannot keep**, for example an agent who promises a callback when no callback process exists.

Blueprints are especially useful in banking, insurance and telecom, where most of the work happens out of sight. A customer sees a five-minute branch visit; the blueprint may reveal eight backstage steps across three departments and two systems. That is where the delays and errors live.

cards.title: Blueprinting an online order return
cards.body:
An online fashion retailer in Lahore found that returns produced a large share of its negative reviews. The CX team blueprinted the return process.

**Customer actions:** requests return on WhatsApp → sends photos → waits for pickup → hands parcel to rider → waits for refund.

**Frontstage:** WhatsApp agent replies, confirms eligibility, books pickup.

**Line of visibility**

**Backstage:** agent copies details into a spreadsheet → warehouse checks the spreadsheet twice a day → courier is booked manually → item is inspected on arrival → finance processes refund weekly.

**Support processes:** courier partner portal, payment gateway, spreadsheet shared by email.

**Findings:**

- **Fail point:** manual copying into the spreadsheet caused wrong addresses in a noticeable share of pickups.
- **Wait point:** refunds were processed only once a week, so a customer who returned an item on Thursday could wait over a week more.
- **Broken promise:** agents told customers "refund in 3 days", but the backstage weekly cycle made that impossible.

**Fixes:** a simple return form feeding the courier portal directly, daily refund runs, and agents trained to quote the realistic timeline. Return-related negative reviews fell sharply over the next two months.

The frontline was not the problem. The blueprint showed the failures were all below the line of visibility.

cards.title: Walk the journey yourself
cards.body: Before any workshop, go through the journey as a customer: open the account, call the helpline, try the app, visit a branch outside your own city. Record times, steps and feelings. Senior leaders who do this once often become the strongest supporters of CX change. Combine it with formal mystery shopping for a structured, repeatable view.

cards.question: In a service blueprint for issuing a replacement debit card, where would "card is printed at the central card unit and dispatched by courier" appear?
options: Physical evidence
Customer actions
Frontstage actions
Backstage actions or support processes, below the line of visibility
cards.explanation: Card printing and dispatch happen out of the customer's sight, so they sit below the line of visibility as backstage or support activity. The card the customer finally receives would be physical evidence, but the printing process itself is not.

cards.title: Take-aways from the Bazaar of Voices
items: Combine solicited feedback, unsolicited feedback and operational data; each reveals what the others miss.
Low complaint volume does not mean satisfaction, especially where customers avoid confrontation.
Build a small number of needs-based personas from evidence, and avoid stereotypes.
Journey maps start from the customer's goal, show feelings and waits, and must end in owned actions.
Use Pareto, five whys and fishbone analysis to get from pain points to root causes.
Service blueprints expose fail points, wait points and broken promises below the line of visibility.

cards.prompt: Pick one frequent customer complaint in your area. Apply the five whys honestly. Where did you end up, who owns that root cause, and is it inside or outside your team?

quiz.question: Which of these is an example of unsolicited customer feedback?
options: Responses to an SMS survey sent after a branch visit
Answers from a focus group on a new savings product
A one-star app-store review complaining about login failures
Results of a yearly relationship survey
quiz.explanation: An app-store review is given without the company asking. SMS surveys, focus groups and relationship surveys are all solicited feedback.

quiz.question: An insurer wants to understand why customers lapse after the first policy year. Which combination of VoC inputs would give the most complete picture?
options: Lapse data by segment, interviews with lapsed customers, and complaint and claim records
A detailed relationship survey of current policyholders, repeated every quarter for a full year
Social media monitoring of competitor brands
Agent opinions about why customers lapse
quiz.explanation: Combining behavioural data (who lapses), solicited insight from people who actually left and unsolicited and operational records (complaints, claims) gives the fullest view. Surveying only current customers misses those who left; agent opinion alone is one biased source.

quiz.question: A survey asks: "How satisfied were you with the speed and friendliness of our staff?" What is the main problem with this question?
options: It is leading, because it assumes in advance that the staff were both fast and friendly
It should use a 10-point scale instead of a 5-point scale
It is too short to give useful data
It is double-barrelled, so one rating cannot show which aspect is being judged
quiz.explanation: Speed and friendliness are two different things; a customer who found staff friendly but slow cannot answer accurately. The question does not assume an answer, so it is not leading, and scale length is not the issue.

quiz.question: A digital bank's team proposes three personas: "Males 18–25", "Males 26–40" and "Females 18–40". What is the strongest criticism?
options: There should be at least ten personas
They are demographic bands that say nothing about goals, needs or behaviours
Personas should never include gender
They are acceptable, because demographics are easy to measure and link directly to marketing data
quiz.explanation: Useful personas are based on needs, goals and behaviours shown by evidence. Age-gender bands lump together customers who behave very differently. The number of personas and the presence of demographic details are not the core issue.

quiz.question: A journey map of a mobile package change shows that customers feel most anxious in the 24 hours after requesting the change, when they receive no confirmation and are unsure if they will be charged twice. What is the best first improvement?
options: Speed up the backend so that the package change completes in 12 hours instead of 24 hours
Offer a discount on the next package change
Send instant confirmation and a completion message that explains how billing will work
Add more agents to handle the calls from anxious customers
quiz.explanation: The pain is uncertainty during the wait, not the wait itself. Proactive confirmation and clear billing information address the cause cheaply. A faster backend helps but still leaves silence; more agents only absorb symptoms.

quiz.question: Complaint data for a utility company shows: billing errors 410, late connection 160, rude staff 90, meter reading disputes 260, app issues 80. Using Pareto thinking, which two categories should be tackled first?
options: Rude staff and app issues, because they are the quickest to fix and show visible progress
Late connection and rude staff
All five equally, to show customers every issue matters
Billing errors and meter reading disputes, about two-thirds of the total
quiz.explanation: Total = 1,000. Billing errors (410) plus meter disputes (260) = 670, about 67% of complaints. Pareto analysis directs effort to the few causes driving most volume. They may also share a root cause in meter reading.

quiz.question: A team applies the five whys to repeated calls about delayed cheque books and concludes, "Root cause: call-centre agents give poor information." Why is this probably not the real root cause?
options: Agent behaviour is likely a symptom; the deeper cause may be missing tracking data from the courier
The five whys technique can only be used for IT problems
Agents are never responsible for customer problems
Cheque book delays are caused by the courier company, so they are outside the bank's control and cannot be fixed
quiz.explanation: Stopping at people often misses systemic causes. If agents have no tracking data, better scripts will not help. Agents can contribute to problems, so option C overstates; five whys is not limited to IT.

quiz.question: In a service blueprint for a home loan, a branch officer promises the customer "we will call you within two days with an update", but no process or system exists to trigger that call. What type of problem has the blueprint revealed?
options: A physical evidence problem
A frontstage promise that backstage processes cannot keep
A problem with the customer's actions
A persona design error
quiz.explanation: The promise is made frontstage, but no backstage or support process delivers it, so it will often be broken. Blueprints are designed to expose this kind of gap across the line of visibility.

quiz.question: Which statement about journey maps and service blueprints is correct?
options: Journey maps are used for digital channels such as apps, and blueprints for physical channels such as branches
Blueprints replace the need to talk to customers
Journey maps show internal handovers in detail, while blueprints show only emotions
Journey maps show the customer's experience; blueprints add the activities that deliver it
quiz.explanation: A journey map views the experience from outside; a blueprint extends it to show what the organisation does, visible and invisible, to deliver each step. Both apply to any channel and neither replaces customer research.

quiz.question: A bank's branch network in southern Sindh receives far fewer written complaints than branches in Islamabad, though customer numbers are similar. A manager concludes the southern branches deliver better service. What is the best response?
options: Agree, and use the southern branches as the benchmark when setting service standards for the whole network
Reduce complaint channels in Islamabad to lower the volume
Treat it as a hypothesis; fewer complaints may reflect access or reluctance, not better service
Ignore complaint data because it is unreliable
quiz.explanation: Complaint volume depends on how easy and acceptable it is to complain, not only on service quality. Check with other sources such as operational data, surveys in local languages and mystery shopping before concluding. Ignoring complaint data entirely goes too far.

sessions.title: Delivering Service Excellence: Empathy, Complaints, Recovery and Omnichannel
sessions.summary: Build the practical skills of excellent service: clear and empathetic communication, a structured way to handle complaints and difficult customers, service recovery that restores trust, bilingual and cultural awareness, and consistent omnichannel service.
objectives: Use active listening, positive language and genuine empathy in Urdu and English
Handle a complaint using the five-step ASAAN approach
De-escalate difficult customers while protecting staff dignity and safety
Design service recovery that is fair in outcome, process and treatment
Deliver consistent service across branch, call centre, WhatsApp and app

cards.title: Communication that customers trust
cards.body:
Most service failures involve some communication failure: a customer who did not understand, an expectation set wrongly or a message delivered coldly. Five habits make a large difference.

**1. Listen to understand, not to reply.** Let the customer finish. Take notes. Many agents start solving before they know the real problem, and the customer has to repeat themselves.

**2. Confirm your understanding.** "So the payment left your account on the 3rd, but the school says it has not received it. Is that right?" This shows you listened and prevents solving the wrong problem.

**3. Use plain language.** Avoid internal terms such as "TAT", "CBS", "maker-checker" or "the case is in the queue". Say "the team that approves this usually takes two working days".

**4. Use positive, action-focused language.** Lead with what you can do.

| Instead of | Try |
|---|---|
| "That's not my department." | "Let me connect you to the right person and explain your case to them." |
| "You should have read the terms." | "Let me explain how this charge works and what options you have." |
| "I can't do anything until Monday." | "The team works again on Monday; I will submit it now so it is first in line." |

**5. Set honest expectations.** Give a realistic time, not the one the customer wants to hear. Under-promise slightly and deliver. A missed promise creates a second complaint on top of the first.

**Tone matters as much as words.** On the phone, customers judge tone within seconds. Smiling while speaking, a steady pace and using the customer's name with an appropriate title ("Khan sahib", "Mrs Javed") all signal respect. In writing, read your message once from the customer's side before sending.

cards.title: Empathy that is real, not scripted
cards.body:
**Empathy** is understanding how a situation feels for the customer and showing that understanding. It is different from **sympathy** (feeling sorry for someone) and different from **agreement** (accepting that the company was wrong). You can empathise with a customer's frustration even when the policy was correctly applied.

**Three elements of empathetic responses:**

1. **Name the situation specifically.** "Your salary was due today and the transfer has not arrived, and rent is due tomorrow."
2. **Acknowledge the feeling.** "I can understand why that is worrying."
3. **Move to action.** "Let me check exactly where the transfer is right now."

**Why scripted empathy fails:** customers quickly recognise a stock phrase like "I understand your frustration" repeated in the same tone on every call, especially when the agent then does nothing different. Specific acknowledgement, linked to the customer's own words, feels genuine.

**In Urdu,** empathy often comes through respectful address and warmth: "Main samajh sakta/sakti hoon, yeh waqai pareshani wali baat hai" said sincerely, followed by action, works far better than a translated English script. Use "aap" consistently.

**Empathy has limits.** It is not:

- Promising what you cannot deliver to calm someone down.
- Agreeing that a colleague was incompetent.
- Spending 40 minutes on a call that needs five. Empathy should make resolution faster, not replace it.

Research on effort shows that customers value a quick, correct resolution most. Empathy works best as the bridge that makes the customer willing to follow your solution.

cards.question: A customer's car-insurance claim was correctly declined because the driver had no valid licence. The customer is upset. Which response shows empathy without misleading the customer?
options: "I completely agree, the decision is unfair. I will try to get it reversed."
"Sir, the policy is clear. There is nothing more to discuss."
"I understand this is a big financial blow after an accident. Let me explain exactly why the claim was declined and what options you have."
"I understand your frustration. Please hold."
cards.explanation: Option C acknowledges the specific impact and then moves to honest explanation and options. Option A falsely suggests the decision was wrong and raises false hope; B is cold; D is a stock phrase with no follow-through.

cards.title: Handling complaints: the ASAAN approach
cards.body:
A complaint is a customer telling you, for free, where your experience is broken. Most unhappy customers never complain; they simply leave. Treat each complaint as a gift and handle it with a consistent structure. This course uses a five-step approach called **ASAAN** ("easy" in Urdu), because the goal is to make resolution easy for the customer.

**A: Acknowledge.** Thank the customer for raising it, listen without interrupting and acknowledge the feeling. Do not defend or explain yet.

**S: Seek understanding.** Ask open questions, then closed ones to confirm facts. Check the record. Separate what the customer wants (a refund, an apology, a fix, to be heard) from what happened.

**A: Apologise appropriately.** Apologise sincerely for the experience. If the company is clearly at fault, own it plainly. If facts are unclear, apologise for the inconvenience without admitting fault you have not established. Never blame a colleague or another department in front of the customer.

**A: Agree and act.** Offer a solution or options, agree on what will happen and by when, and act on it immediately where possible. If you cannot resolve it yourself, take ownership of the handover: explain the case to the next person so the customer does not have to.

**N: Notify and follow through.** Tell the customer what was done and confirm they are satisfied. Record the complaint and its root cause so it can feed improvement. In regulated sectors, also provide the complaint reference number and the escalation route if they remain unhappy.

The structure keeps you steady when a customer is upset, and the record keeps the organisation learning.

cards.title: ASAAN at a branch counter in Rawalpindi
cards.body:
Mr Tariq Mehmood, a retired schoolteacher, arrives at a branch angry. His ATM card was declined when he tried to withdraw his pension, and he has had to borrow from a neighbour.

**Acknowledge.** The customer services officer, Hina, stands to greet him, offers a seat and says: "Mehmood sahib, thank you for coming in. Having to borrow money when your own pension is in the account is very upsetting. Please tell me what happened." She lets him speak for two minutes without interrupting.

**Seek understanding.** She asks when he last used the account, whether he received any SMS, and whether anything changed recently. Checking the system, she finds the pension has been credited, but the account was marked dormant because he had made no customer-initiated transactions for a long period while he was staying with his son abroad, so withdrawals were blocked.

**Apologise.** "I am sorry. We should have reminded you clearly before the account was marked inactive, and you should not have found out like this."

**Agree and act.** She explains the steps and completes the re-activation with his CNIC and biometric verification on the spot, so he can withdraw his pension at the counter immediately. His ATM card needs a separate unblock request, and she tells him honestly: "The card is usually working again within one working day. I will call you tomorrow by 12 o'clock either way."

**Notify and follow through.** The next day at 11:30 she calls to confirm the card is working. She also logs the root cause: pensioners whose only activity is incoming pension credits can be marked dormant without realising it. She raises this with operations, who add a reminder SMS in Urdu for at-risk pension accounts.

Mr Mehmood later tells the branch manager he will keep his account there.

cards.title: Difficult customers and de-escalation
cards.body:
Most customers who seem "difficult" are frightened, exhausted or have already been let down several times. Some are genuinely abusive. Your approach should differ.

**De-escalating an angry customer:**

- **Stay calm and lower your voice slightly.** People unconsciously match tone.
- **Let them vent** before problem-solving. Interrupting an angry person usually extends the anger.
- **Use their name and respectful address.**
- **Agree with what you can**: "You are right that you should have received an SMS."
- **Move to specifics**: "Let me write down the dates so we can trace this properly."
- **Offer choices**, which restore a sense of control: "I can call you back in one hour with an answer, or you can wait while I check. Which is better for you?"
- **Change the setting** if needed: move from a crowded counter to a private desk.

**Common situations:**

- **"Do you know who I am?"** Stay respectful and consistent. Treat everyone with high courtesy, but apply the same rules. Escalate to a supervisor if the customer insists; do not bend policy under pressure.
- **Repeat or unreasonable demands.** Restate clearly what you can and cannot do and why, offer the formal escalation route, and document the interaction.
- **Abuse, threats or harassment.** No staff member should accept abusive or threatening language or sexual harassment. Give one calm warning on the phone ("I want to help you, but I cannot continue if this language continues"), then end the call per policy. In person, call a supervisor or security. Report and record it.

**Organisations must back their staff** with a clear unacceptable-behaviour policy, supervisor support and debriefs after hard interactions. Without that, burnout and staff turnover follow.

cards.title: Phrases that make things worse
cards.body:
Avoid these, in any language:

- "Calm down." It implies the customer's feelings are wrong.
- "That's our policy." Explain the reason behind it instead.
- "You must have done something wrong." Investigate before assigning blame.
- "I'm new here." The customer does not need to hear it; find help instead.
- "Aap ko pehle batana chahiye tha." ("You should have told us earlier.") Blame does not solve anything now.

cards.title: Service recovery: restoring trust after failure
cards.body:
**Service recovery** is what an organisation does after it fails a customer. Done well, it can preserve or even strengthen the relationship; done badly, it turns an annoyed customer into an active detractor.

Research on complaint handling shows that customers judge recovery on **three kinds of fairness**:

1. **Fair outcome**: did I get a reasonable result? A correction, refund, replacement or compensation proportional to the harm.
2. **Fair process**: was it handled quickly, with clear steps, without making me chase, and with a single point of ownership?
3. **Fair treatment**: was I treated with respect, honesty and empathy, and given an explanation?

A generous refund delivered after six weeks of chasing and rude emails still feels unfair. A modest remedy given quickly, honestly and warmly often satisfies.

**Principles of strong recovery:**

- **Speed matters.** Value of recovery drops as time passes.
- **Empower the front line** to fix common problems on the spot, within clear limits (for example, waiving a fee up to a set amount).
- **Match the remedy to the harm.** Reverse the financial impact fully; add a gesture when the inconvenience was significant.
- **Fix the cause**, so the failure does not repeat.

**The service recovery paradox** is the idea that a customer whose problem is resolved excellently may end up more loyal than one who never had a problem. Studies show this happens only sometimes: usually when the failure was not severe, was not repeated, and the recovery was outstanding. It disappears after a second failure. Never rely on it as a strategy; preventing failures remains far better.

cards.title: Recovering from a network outage
cards.body:
A fibre broadband provider in Islamabad suffers a 30-hour outage in one sector after a construction company cuts a cable. About 4,000 home customers are affected, many of whom work from home.

**Poor recovery (what happened in a previous outage):** The helpline gave a generic message, "technical team is working". Customers who called were told to restart their routers. No compensation was offered unless a customer complained repeatedly, and then amounts varied by agent. Social media filled with angry posts.

**Better recovery (this time):**

- **Fair process:** within two hours, an SMS and WhatsApp message in English and Urdu explained the cause, the area affected and an estimated restoration time, with updates every six hours. The helpline greeting was updated so callers in the area heard the status immediately and were not asked to restart routers.
- **Fair treatment:** messages took responsibility for the disruption even though a third party cut the cable, and acknowledged the impact on people working and studying from home.
- **Fair outcome:** every affected customer automatically received a pro-rata credit for the downtime plus two extra days of service, without needing to ask. Business customers received calls from their account managers.
- **Fixing the cause:** the provider agreed a cable-marking and notification arrangement with the local development authority for future construction work.

Repeat calls about the outage were a fraction of the previous incident, and several customers posted publicly that they appreciated the updates. The failure was the same; the recovery changed how it was remembered.

cards.question: A customer receives a full refund of a wrongly charged PKR 3,500 fee, but only after five calls over three weeks, each time explaining the issue again. Which fairness dimension was weakest?
options: Fair outcome, because the refund was too small
Fair process, because the customer had to chase and repeat themselves
None, because the customer received a full refund
Fair treatment, because the agents were probably rude
cards.explanation: The outcome (a full refund) was fair, and nothing suggests rudeness. The process failed: slow, repetitive and without ownership. Customers often judge a slow, repetitive process harshly even when the final outcome is correct.

cards.title: Bilingual and cultural considerations in Pakistan
cards.body:
Pakistani customers move between Urdu, English and regional languages such as Punjabi, Sindhi, Pashto, Saraiki and Balochi, often within one conversation. Service that respects this feels more personal and prevents misunderstandings.

**Language:**

- **Let the customer choose the language** and follow their lead. If they switch to Urdu, switch with them.
- **Do not assume** English proficiency from appearance, or lack of it from accent.
- **Explain financial and technical terms** in everyday Urdu, not literal translations. "Markup" or "profit rate" may need a simple example in rupees.
- **Roman Urdu** is widely used on WhatsApp and SMS. Written replies in Roman Urdu or Urdu script can be appropriate when the customer writes that way, within brand guidelines.
- **Regional language support** in contact centres and branches serving particular areas can significantly reduce effort for customers who are less comfortable in Urdu.

**Respect and courtesy:**

- Use **"aap"** and respectful titles (sahib, sahiba, or the customer's preferred title).
- **Elders** expect visible courtesy: a greeting, a seat, patience. Rushing them reads as disrespect.
- **Gender sensitivity:** some women customers may prefer to deal with a female staff member, a separate queue or a private desk. Offer, do not assume.
- **Religious and seasonal patterns:** contact volumes, branch footfall and emotions spike before Eid, at the start of the month (salaries and pensions), and during Ramadan, when timings change and fatigue is common. Plan staffing and tone accordingly.

**Customers with disabilities and low literacy** need accessible options: step-free entry, help reading forms, voice-based support and patience. Accessibility is part of service, not charity.

cards.title: Omnichannel: one relationship, many doors
cards.body:
Customers now reach organisations through branches, call centres, WhatsApp, apps, websites, social media, agents and retailers. **Multichannel** means offering many channels. **Omnichannel** means those channels work as one, so the customer can start in one and finish in another without starting again.

**What omnichannel looks like for the customer:**

- The branch officer can see that the customer reported the problem on WhatsApp yesterday.
- The same information, fees and policies are given in every channel.
- A request started in the app can be completed at the branch without re-filling forms.
- Complaint references work across channels.

**Channel roles in Pakistan:**

| Channel | Strengths | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|
| Branch / store | Trust, complex needs, cash, elderly customers | Queues, inconsistent advice between branches |
| Call centre | Urgent issues, guidance | Long IVR menus, transfers |
| WhatsApp | Familiar, asynchronous, documents and voice notes | Slow replies, fake accounts impersonating the brand |
| App | Speed, self-service at any hour | Login failures, low digital confidence, connectivity |

**Security is part of the experience.** Fraudsters impersonate banks and telecoms on WhatsApp and calls. Every channel should repeat clear messages, such as "we will never ask for your OTP, PIN or password", and official accounts should be verified so customers can recognise them.

**Digital inclusion.** Pushing every customer to the app saves cost but can exclude elderly, low-literacy or rural customers. Good omnichannel design guides customers to digital where it helps them, keeps an assisted route available and uses staff to build digital confidence.

cards.title: Starting again in every channel
cards.body:
Zainab Hussain in Hyderabad reported an unauthorised transaction on her credit card through the bank's WhatsApp service on Monday evening. The chatbot blocked her card and gave a reference number.

On Tuesday, she called the helpline to ask about a replacement. The agent could not see the WhatsApp conversation and asked her to describe the transaction again, then opened a new dispute with a different reference. On Wednesday, she visited a branch. The officer could not find either reference and asked her to fill in a paper dispute form.

By Thursday, Zainab had three references, had told her story three times and still did not know whether her money would be returned. She posted her experience on social media.

**What the bank changed after reviewing the case:**

- WhatsApp, call-centre and branch staff were given access to a single case view showing all contacts linked to a customer.
- One dispute reference was generated per incident, regardless of channel.
- The chatbot's closing message was improved to explain what happens next, the expected timeline and how to track it.
- Agents were trained to say "I can see you contacted us on WhatsApp yesterday" before asking anything.

The bank already had good individual channels. The failure was that they did not share context, which multiplied the customer's effort and anxiety.

cards.question: Which change best moves a bank from multichannel to omnichannel service?
options: Launching a new chatbot on its website
Opening more branches in smaller cities
Extending call-centre hours to 24/7
Giving all channels a shared view of each customer's recent contacts and open cases
cards.explanation: Omnichannel is about channels working together so customers do not repeat themselves. A shared case view enables that. Adding a chatbot, branches or hours expands individual channels, which is multichannel growth.

cards.title: Take-aways from the Hall of Mended Promises
items: Listen fully, confirm understanding, use plain and positive language, and set honest expectations.
Empathy is specific acknowledgement plus action; it is not agreement or false promises.
ASAAN: Acknowledge, Seek understanding, Apologise appropriately, Agree and act, Notify and follow through.
De-escalate frustration with calm, choices and specifics; never tolerate abuse, and back staff with clear policy.
Recovery is judged on fair outcome, fair process and fair treatment; speed and empowerment matter most.
Follow the customer's language, show visible respect, and plan for seasonal and cultural patterns.
Omnichannel means shared context across channels, consistent answers and security built into every touchpoint.

cards.prompt: Recall a recent complaint you handled or observed. Which ASAAN step was weakest, and which fairness dimension (outcome, process or treatment) did the customer most likely judge harshly?

quiz.question: An agent says to a caller: "The case is pending with CBS ops for maker-checker, TAT is 48 hours." What is the main communication problem?
options: The agent is too formal
The agent should have transferred the call
The timeline is too short
The agent is using internal jargon the customer is unlikely to understand
quiz.explanation: CBS, maker-checker and TAT are internal terms. Plain language would be: "The team that approves this usually takes up to two days." Formality and timeline length are not the issue here.

quiz.question: A customer is angry that her son's university fee transfer has not reached the university two days before the deadline. Which opening is the strongest example of empathy?
options: "I understand your frustration, madam. May I please have your account number and CNIC to check?"
"With the fee deadline in two days, I can see why this is stressful. Let me trace it now."
"Please don't worry, these things always sort themselves out."
"Transfers can take time. You should have sent it earlier."
quiz.explanation: Option B names the specific situation, acknowledges the feeling and moves straight to action. A is a stock phrase, C gives false reassurance, and D blames the customer.

quiz.question: In the ASAAN approach, a branch officer has listened to an upset customer and checked the record, but it is not yet clear whether the bank or the customer made the error. What is the most appropriate apology?
options: Apologise for the trouble caused, without admitting a fault not yet established
Admit that the bank made the error, to calm the customer
Avoid any apology until the investigation is complete, so the bank does not accept liability
Explain that another department is probably responsible
quiz.explanation: ASAAN asks for an appropriate apology: sincere regret for the experience without claiming fault that is not established. Admitting unproven fault can mislead; withholding any apology feels cold; blaming another department breaks trust.

quiz.question: A caller at a telecom helpline has been shouting about repeated billing errors for two minutes. What should the agent do first?
options: Interrupt firmly and ask the caller to calm down
Transfer the call to a supervisor immediately, since supervisors have more authority to resolve billing errors
Let the caller finish, acknowledge what went wrong, then move to the details
End the call because the caller is shouting
quiz.explanation: Shouting from frustration is not abuse. Letting the customer vent, then acknowledging and moving to specifics, de-escalates. "Calm down" inflames, transfers add effort, and ending the call is reserved for abusive or threatening behaviour after a warning.

quiz.question: A customer on the phone begins using abusive personal language towards the agent after being told his loan application was declined. According to good practice, what should the agent do?
options: Continue the call silently until the customer finishes
Respond in the same tone so the customer realises it is unacceptable
Reverse the loan decision or promise a review, so that the conflict ends and the customer calms down
Give one calm warning, then end the call per policy and record it if the abuse continues
quiz.explanation: Staff should not accept abuse. A calm warning gives the customer a chance to continue respectfully; ending the call per policy and recording it protects the agent. Matching the tone escalates; reversing a credit decision under pressure is improper.

quiz.question: An e-commerce company refunds customers fully for damaged deliveries, but only after a 30-day investigation in which customers must email photos twice and are given no updates. Satisfaction with refunds is low. What is the best explanation?
options: The refunds are too small
The process and treatment are perceived as unfair even though the outcome is fair
Customers do not value refunds
Photos should not be requested at all
quiz.explanation: The outcome (a full refund) is fair, but the slow, repetitive, silent process undermines the experience. Requesting a photo once can be reasonable; the problem is duplication, delay and lack of updates.

quiz.question: A hotel guest's room was not ready at check-in for two hours. The hotel apologised, upgraded the room and gave a complimentary dinner. The guest later posts a very positive review. Six months later, the same thing happens again, with the same remedy, and the guest posts a negative review. What does this best illustrate?
options: The guest was being unreasonable the second time
Room upgrades are an ineffective recovery remedy, because guests expect them as standard at good hotels
Recovery can lift loyalty after one failure, but the effect fades when failures repeat
Complimentary dinners should be replaced with cash compensation
quiz.explanation: Excellent recovery may boost loyalty after a one-off failure, but a repeated failure signals that the problem is systemic, so the effect vanishes. This is why prevention and root-cause fixes matter more than recovery gestures.

quiz.question: An elderly customer at a branch in Quetta starts speaking in Pashto after struggling with Urdu forms. No staff member at the counter speaks Pashto. What is the best response?
options: Get a Pashto-speaking colleague, or help fill the form in simple Urdu, and log the language need
Politely ask the customer to come back with a family member who can read and speak Urdu fluently
Hand the customer an English version of the form
Continue in fast Urdu, since it is the national language
quiz.explanation: Following the customer's language need where possible, and assisting patiently otherwise, reduces effort and respects the customer. Logging the need helps fix the root cause (staffing for local languages). The other options shift effort to the customer.

quiz.question: A bank's WhatsApp channel receives messages from customers who say they were contacted by "bank staff" on WhatsApp asking for their OTP. What is the most appropriate CX response?
options: Close the WhatsApp channel to avoid confusion
Ask affected customers to share the OTP they received with the official channel so it can be verified
Leave fraud messaging to the fraud team, since it is not a CX issue
Warn in every channel that OTPs are never requested, verify the official account, offer fast blocking
quiz.explanation: Security is part of the experience. Consistent warnings, a verifiable official account and a quick blocking route protect customers. Closing the channel removes a useful service; asking for OTPs, even officially, reinforces the scam pattern; CX cannot ignore fraud.

quiz.question: A telecom's call-centre agents are allowed to waive late-payment fees only after supervisor approval, which takes an average of 25 minutes per request. Most waivers are below PKR 500 and nearly all are approved. What is the best recommendation?
options: Remove the ability to waive fees entirely
Let agents waive fees up to a set limit, with logging and audit
Add more supervisors to the floor so that approvals take five minutes instead of twenty-five
Ask customers to submit waiver requests by email
quiz.explanation: Empowerment within clear limits speeds recovery and reduces effort, while logging and audits manage risk. Since almost all small waivers are approved, the approval step adds delay but little control. More supervisors adds cost; email adds effort.

sessions.title: Measuring CX: NPS, CSAT, CES, FCR and Closing the Loop
sessions.summary: Learn to calculate and interpret the core CX metrics correctly, pair them with operational measures, read changes with statistical caution, close the loop with customers and the organisation, and recognise when metrics are being gamed.
