objectives: Calculate NPS, CSAT, CES and first-contact resolution correctly from raw data
Interpret metric changes with attention to sample size, scale and survey design
Design inner-loop and outer-loop processes that turn feedback into action
Recognise metric gaming and design balanced measures that resist it

cards.title: What to measure and why
cards.body:
CX measurement has one purpose: to help the organisation decide what to fix and whether its fixes worked. A score that nobody acts on is decoration.

Useful measures fall into three groups:

**1. Perception metrics** capture what customers think and feel:
- **NPS (Net Promoter Score)**: likelihood to recommend, used as a loyalty indicator.
- **CSAT (Customer Satisfaction)**: satisfaction with an interaction or product.
- **CES (Customer Effort Score)**: how easy it was to get something done.

**2. Operational metrics** capture what happened:
- First-contact resolution (FCR), repeat contact rate, complaint resolution time, average handling time (AHT), queue waiting time, abandonment rate, app failure rate.

**3. Outcome metrics** capture business results:
- Retention and churn, share of wallet, products per customer, revenue per customer, cost to serve.

**The real insight comes from linking the three.** For example: customers who needed more than one contact to resolve an issue (operational) give lower CES and NPS (perception) and churn at a higher rate (outcome). That chain is what convinces finance to fund a fix.

**Relationship versus transactional measurement:**

| | Relationship | Transactional |
|---|---|---|
| When | Periodically (e.g. twice a year) | Soon after an interaction |
| Question | Overall view of the company | This call, visit, delivery or claim |
| Best use | Tracking loyalty and strategy | Fixing specific processes and coaching staff |
| Typical metric | NPS | CSAT, CES, transactional NPS |

No single metric is enough. Each answers a different question, and each can be misread or gamed when used alone.

cards.title: Net Promoter Score: calculation and meaning
cards.body:
NPS asks: **"On a scale of 0 to 10, how likely are you to recommend [company] to a friend or colleague?"**

Responses are grouped:

- **Promoters:** 9 or 10
- **Passives:** 7 or 8
- **Detractors:** 0 to 6

**NPS = % promoters − % detractors.**

Passives count in the total number of responses but are not added or subtracted. The result is a number between **−100** (everyone a detractor) and **+100** (everyone a promoter). It is reported as a plain number such as +32, not as a percentage.

**Key points for correct interpretation:**

- **Two companies with the same NPS can be very different.** 50% promoters and 10% detractors gives +40; so does 40% promoters and 0% detractors. Always look at the distribution.
- **Moving passives to promoters raises NPS; moving detractors to passives also raises it.** Reducing detractors is often the quicker win, because detractors usually have identifiable problems.
- **Benchmarks vary greatly by industry and country.** Banks, telecoms and utilities often score lower than hospitality or retail. Compare with your own trend and with competitors measured the same way, not with global figures from other sectors.
- **Cultural response styles matter.** In some markets customers rarely give a 10 even when very happy; in others they score generously to be polite. Track your own trend over time rather than relying on absolute values.
- **Always ask why.** The follow-up open question ("What is the main reason for your score?") is where most of the value lies.

NPS is a useful loyalty indicator, but it measures intention, not behaviour. Check that promoters actually stay and buy more in your own data.

cards.title: Calculating NPS for a mobile operator
cards.body:
A mobile operator surveys 500 postpaid customers in Karachi.

| Score | Customers |
|---|---|
| 9–10 (promoters) | 190 |
| 7–8 (passives) | 160 |
| 0–6 (detractors) | 150 |
| **Total** | **500** |

**Step 1: percentages.** Promoters = 190 ÷ 500 = **38%**. Detractors = 150 ÷ 500 = **30%**. Passives = 160 ÷ 500 = 32%.

**Step 2: subtract.** NPS = 38 − 30 = **+8**.

**Common errors to avoid:**

- Subtracting counts instead of percentages (190 − 150 = 40) gives a meaningless number.
- Excluding passives from the denominator: 190 ÷ 340 = 55.9% and 150 ÷ 340 = 44.1% gives +11.8, which overstates the score.
- Treating 7 as a detractor or 8 as a promoter.

**What-if analysis.** The CX team reads the comments of detractors and finds that 60 of the 150 mention dropped calls in two specific areas. If network fixes moved those 60 to passives, detractors would fall to 90 (18%) and NPS would rise to 38 − 18 = **+20**, a twelve-point gain without creating a single new promoter.

If instead 50 passives became promoters, promoters would rise to 240 (48%) and NPS would be 48 − 30 = **+18**.

Both paths help, but the detractor path is linked to a specific, fixable cause with an owner (the network team), which makes it the better first investment.

cards.question: A bank receives 80 NPS responses: 36 promoters, 24 passives and 20 detractors. What is its NPS?
cards.explanation: Promoters 36 ÷ 80 = 45%; detractors 20 ÷ 80 = 25%; NPS = 45 − 25 = +20. +16 subtracts counts; +28.6 wrongly excludes passives from the denominator (36 ÷ 56 − 20 ÷ 56).

cards.title: CSAT and Customer Effort Score
cards.body:
**CSAT** asks how satisfied the customer was, usually with a specific interaction. The most common format is a 5-point scale (1 = very dissatisfied, 5 = very satisfied).

There are two common ways to report it, and you must always say which you use:

- **Top-two-box CSAT:** the percentage of respondents who chose 4 or 5. **CSAT = (number of 4s and 5s ÷ total responses) × 100.** This is the most widely used convention and the one used in this course unless stated otherwise.
- **Average score:** the mean rating, such as 4.1 out of 5.

CSAT is easy to understand and good for coaching and process fixes. Its weakness is that "satisfied" customers may still leave; satisfaction is not loyalty.

**CES** measures how easy it was for the customer to get what they needed. Effort is a strong predictor of disloyalty: high-effort experiences push customers away more reliably than delight pulls them in.

A common modern format asks customers to rate agreement with a statement such as **"[Company] made it easy for me to handle my issue"** on a 7-point scale (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree). It can be reported as:

- **An average**, for example 5.6 out of 7 (higher = easier), or
- **The percentage who agree** (scores 5, 6 or 7).

Older versions asked "How much effort did you personally have to put forth?" on a 1–5 scale where **lower is better**. Because direction differs between versions, **always state the scale and direction** in every report, and never compare scores collected on different scales.

**Which to use where:** CES after service and problem-solving interactions; CSAT after transactions and for staff coaching; NPS for relationship tracking.

cards.title: Calculating CSAT and CES for a helpline
cards.body:
A health insurer's helpline collects two questions after each call in one week.

**CSAT (1–5 scale), 400 responses:**

| Score | 5 | 4 | 3 | 2 | 1 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Count | 180 | 120 | 50 | 30 | 20 |

- **Top-two-box CSAT** = (180 + 120) ÷ 400 = 300 ÷ 400 = **75%**.
- **Average CSAT** = (5×180 + 4×120 + 3×50 + 2×30 + 1×20) ÷ 400 = (900 + 480 + 150 + 60 + 20) ÷ 400 = 1,610 ÷ 400 = **4.03 out of 5** (rounded).

**CES ("The insurer made it easy to handle my issue", 1–7, higher = easier), 400 responses:**

| Score | 7 | 6 | 5 | 4 | 3 | 2 | 1 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Count | 100 | 120 | 60 | 40 | 40 | 20 | 20 |

- **Average CES** = (700 + 720 + 300 + 160 + 120 + 40 + 20) ÷ 400 = 2,060 ÷ 400 = **5.15 out of 7**.
- **% agree (5–7)** = (100 + 120 + 60) ÷ 400 = 280 ÷ 400 = **70%**.

**Interpretation:** three in four callers are satisfied, but one in five (80 of 400) rated ease at 3 or below. When the team filtered by call reason, the low-effort scores clustered around **hospital pre-authorisation calls**, where callers were transferred between the helpline and the medical team. Satisfaction with agents stayed high on those calls: agents were courteous, but the process forced effort. The fix belonged to the pre-authorisation process, not to agent coaching.

cards.question: On a 5-point CSAT survey of 250 customers, 90 chose 5, 85 chose 4, 40 chose 3, 20 chose 2 and 15 chose 1. What is the top-two-box CSAT?
cards.explanation: Top-two-box = (90 + 85) ÷ 250 = 175 ÷ 250 = 70%. 36% counts only the 5s; 86% wrongly includes the neutral 3s; 3.8 is roughly the average score (3.86), which is a different way of reporting.

cards.title: First-contact resolution and operational metrics
cards.body:
**First-contact resolution (FCR)** is the share of customer issues resolved in the first contact, without the customer needing to come back. It is one of the operational measures most closely linked to satisfaction and effort.

**FCR = issues resolved at first contact ÷ total issues × 100.**

The hard part is defining "resolved". Common methods:

- **Repeat-contact method:** an issue counts as resolved at first contact if the same customer does not contact again about the same issue within a set window (often 7 days, sometimes longer for complex products). This is usually more reliable than agent judgement.
- **Customer-reported:** the survey asks, "Was your issue resolved?" Useful, but only for those who respond.
- **Agent-reported:** the agent ticks "resolved". Easy but easily inflated.

Always count **issues**, not calls: a customer who calls three times about one problem is one issue with two repeat contacts, not three issues.

**Other operational measures and their traps:**

| Metric | What it tells you | Trap if used alone |
|---|---|---|
| Average handling time (AHT) | Efficiency, staffing needs | Agents rush and customers call back |
| Abandonment rate | Callers giving up in the queue | Hidden by long IVR menus that delay queue entry |
| Complaint resolution time | Speed of complaint handling | Cases closed early without a real fix |
| Repeat contact rate | Failure demand | Customers who give up and leave are not counted |

**Pair metrics so that one checks another.** AHT with FCR. Complaint closure time with reopened complaints. Sales conversion with complaints about mis-selling. A balanced set makes it much harder to improve one number by damaging the experience.

cards.title: Read changes with statistical caution
cards.body:
Small samples swing wildly. With 50 NPS responses, a single customer moving from detractor to promoter changes NPS by 4 points (2 ÷ 50 × 100). A monthly branch NPS based on 30 responses can rise or fall 10 points by chance alone.

Before celebrating or punishing:

- Check the **number of responses** and look at the trend over several periods.
- Watch **response rates** and who responds. If only angry or only delighted customers answer, the score is biased.
- Compare like with like: same question, scale, channel and timing.
- Report ranges or rolling averages for small units such as individual branches or agents.

cards.title: Closing the loop: inner and outer
cards.body:
Collecting feedback creates an expectation. Customers who take time to complain or rate you badly and hear nothing back conclude that nobody listens. **Closing the loop** means acting on feedback at two levels.

**The inner loop (individual customers):**

- Low scores and serious comments trigger an alert to a named owner, usually the team lead or branch manager responsible.
- The owner contacts the customer within a set time, for example **two working days** for detractors.
- The goal of the call is to understand, fix the specific issue if possible, and thank the customer, not to argue about the score or ask them to change it.
- The outcome and the root cause are recorded.

**The outer loop (the organisation):**

- Root causes from many inner-loop calls, complaints and surveys are grouped and prioritised (Pareto again).
- Each major cause gets a **cross-functional owner**, an action plan and a deadline.
- Progress is reviewed in a regular CX forum with senior leaders, so fixes that need policy, IT or budget decisions actually happen.
- When a fix is made, customers are told: "You told us the bill was confusing; we have redesigned it." This builds trust in the feedback process itself.

**Why both loops matter:** the inner loop repairs relationships one at a time but never stops the flow of new problems. The outer loop removes causes but is slow and invisible to the individual customer. Mature CX programmes run both, with the inner loop feeding the outer.

**A good inner-loop call also teaches the frontline.** Managers who call detractors themselves quickly learn which policies and processes create the most pain.

cards.title: Closing the loop at a general insurer
cards.body:
A general insurer in Lahore surveys motor-insurance customers after each claim. Monthly, about 15% of respondents score 0–6 on the NPS question.

**Inner loop:** Each detractor response creates a task for the claims team lead in that region, who must call within two working days. Team lead Usman Khalid calls Mr Asad Raza, who scored 3. Mr Raza explains that his claim was paid, but the surveyor visited three days late and the workshop kept his car for 19 days waiting for approval of a single extra part. Usman apologises, explains why the extra approval was needed, and arranges a small goodwill gesture under his authority. He records two causes: surveyor scheduling and slow approval of supplementary estimates.

**Outer loop:** At the monthly CX forum, the claims head reviews coded causes from all detractor calls:

- Supplementary estimate approvals: 34% of detractor comments
- Surveyor scheduling: 22%
- Unclear depreciation deductions: 18%
- Other causes: 26%

The forum agrees three actions with owners and deadlines: approval authority for supplementary estimates below a set amount is delegated to surveyors (claims operations); surveyor booking moves to a shared calendar with SMS confirmation (claims IT); and a one-page Urdu and English explanation of depreciation is sent with every claim estimate (product and compliance).

Three months later, average repair-to-approval time has fallen, detractor share among claimants has dropped, and the insurer has sent a short message to customers who raised these issues explaining what changed.

cards.title: Metric gaming and how to prevent it
cards.body:
When a measure becomes a target, people find ways to hit the target that do not improve the reality it was meant to track. This is often called **Goodhart's law**, and CX metrics are especially vulnerable.

**Common forms of gaming:**

- **Survey begging:** "Please give me 10, my bonus depends on it." Scores rise; the experience does not.
- **Selective surveying:** only happy customers receive the survey link, or agents can choose which calls are surveyed.
- **Excluding bad cases:** "special" or "exceptional" cases removed from the data.
- **Premature closure:** complaints marked resolved before the customer agrees, to meet a closure-time target.
- **Call avoidance:** transferring or disconnecting difficult calls to protect handling time or FCR.
- **Discouraging complaints:** staff persuade customers not to log a formal complaint so the count stays low.

**Warning signs:**

- Scores that rise sharply while complaints, repeat contacts or churn do not improve.
- Unusually uniform scores (almost all 10s) for one branch or agent.
- Very low response rates for one unit compared with others.
- Big differences between agent-reported and customer-reported resolution.

**Prevention:**

- Send surveys automatically, based on random or complete samples, not staff choice.
- **Pair metrics** so that gaming one shows up in another.
- Use scores for **learning and coaching first**; be careful about tying individual pay directly to small-sample scores.
- Audit regularly and make it clear that gaming is a conduct issue.
- Reward improvement in root causes, not just score movement.

Gaming is usually a symptom of targets that are unrealistic or unfair. Fix the design, not only the behaviour.

cards.title: The branch with perfect scores
cards.body:
A consumer bank in the north runs a branch-level CSAT league table, and branch managers receive a bonus for being in the top ten. One branch in Gujranwala reaches 98% top-two-box CSAT for three consecutive months, far above the network average of 82%.

The regional CX analyst, Mehwish Anjum, checks the data before the branch is celebrated:

- The branch's **survey response rate** is 4%, against a network average of 15%.
- Most responses come from customers whose mobile numbers were **updated at the branch** on the day of the visit.
- **Complaints** logged in the central system from that branch's customers rose 30% over the same period.
- A mystery shopper reports being told, "Sir, please rate us 5, it really helps our branch."

Mehwish's conclusion: the survey process at the branch was being steered towards satisfied customers, and some unhappy customers were going straight to the central complaint line instead.

**What the bank changed:**

- Surveys are now triggered automatically from the core system for every eligible transaction, using the number already on record.
- League tables show response rate, complaint rate and CSAT side by side.
- The bonus is based on a balanced scorecard, including mystery shopping and complaint resolution quality, rather than CSAT alone.

The branch's CSAT fell to 80% under the new method, close to the network average. The branch manager was coached rather than dismissed, because the incentive design had encouraged the behaviour.

cards.question: A contact centre's FCR, reported by agents ticking "resolved", has risen from 70% to 88% in three months, but repeat calls within 7 days on the same issue have not changed. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Agent-reported resolution is being inflated, so the improvement is probably not real
Customers are calling back for unrelated reasons
The repeat-call data must be wrong because FCR improved
FCR and repeat calls are unrelated measures
cards.explanation: If issues were truly being resolved first time, repeat contacts on the same issue would fall. Unchanged repeat calls alongside rising agent-reported FCR point to inflated self-reporting. The repeat-contact method is usually more reliable.

cards.title: Take-aways from the Observatory of Signals
items: NPS = % promoters (9–10) − % detractors (0–6); passives stay in the denominator; range −100 to +100.
Top-two-box CSAT = share of 4s and 5s on a 5-point scale; always state whether you report a percentage or an average.
CES measures ease; state the scale and direction, and never compare scores from different scales.
FCR counts issues, not calls; the repeat-contact method is more reliable than agent self-reporting.
Small samples swing widely: check response counts, rates and trends before drawing conclusions.
Close the inner loop with individuals quickly and the outer loop on root causes with owners and deadlines.
Pair metrics, automate surveys and use scores for learning to prevent gaming.

cards.prompt: Which CX metric does your team watch most closely? How exactly is it calculated, how many responses sit behind it, and how could someone improve the number without improving the customer's experience?

quiz.question: A retailer receives 200 NPS responses: 110 scored 9–10, 50 scored 7–8 and 40 scored 0–6. What is the NPS?
quiz.explanation: Promoters 110 ÷ 200 = 55%; detractors 40 ÷ 200 = 20%; NPS = 55 − 20 = +35. +70 subtracts counts; +55 is the promoter share alone; +46.7 excludes passives from the denominator.

quiz.question: A 5-point CSAT survey of 400 customers gives: 5 = 180, 4 = 120, 3 = 50, 2 = 30, 1 = 20. Which pair of results is correct?
options: Top-two-box CSAT 87.5%; average about 4.03
Top-two-box CSAT 45%; average 4.5
Top-two-box CSAT 75%; average about 4.03
Top-two-box CSAT 75%; average 3.0
quiz.explanation: Top-two-box = (180 + 120) ÷ 400 = 75%. Average = (900 + 480 + 150 + 60 + 20) ÷ 400 = 1,610 ÷ 400 ≈ 4.03. 87.5% wrongly includes the 3s; 45% counts only the 5s; 3.0 is the scale midpoint, not the average.

quiz.question: A bank uses a 7-point CES question ("The bank made it easy to handle my request", 1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree). From 100 responses: 7 = 30, 6 = 40, 5 = 20, 4 = 5, 3 = 5. What is the average CES?
quiz.explanation: (7×30 + 6×40 + 5×20 + 4×5 + 3×5) ÷ 100 = (210 + 240 + 100 + 20 + 15) ÷ 100 = 585 ÷ 100 = 5.85. On this scale higher means easier, so this is a fairly positive result. 90% of respondents agreed (scores 5–7).

quiz.question: In one month, a contact centre handles 10,000 calls relating to 4,000 unique customer issues. For 3,000 of those issues the customer did not contact again about the same issue within 7 days. Using the repeat-contact method, what is FCR?
quiz.explanation: FCR counts issues, not calls: 3,000 resolved at first contact ÷ 4,000 issues = 75%. 30% divides by total calls (3,000 ÷ 10,000); 40% is issues ÷ calls, which is not a resolution measure.

quiz.question: A branch's quarterly NPS rose from +20 to +24. Each quarter is based on about 50 responses. The area manager wants to give the branch an award for improvement. What is the best advice?
options: Treat it as normal variation: with 50 responses one customer can move NPS by 4 points
Approve the award, since a four-point rise in NPS within one quarter is a significant improvement
Reduce the branch's survey sample to avoid confusion
Convert the NPS to CSAT, which is more stable
quiz.explanation: With 50 responses, one detractor becoming a promoter changes NPS by 4 points (2 ÷ 50 × 100). A four-point move is well within chance variation. Smaller samples make it worse, and NPS cannot simply be converted to CSAT.

quiz.question: Company X has 60% promoters and 20% detractors. Company Y has 45% promoters and 5% detractors. Which statement is correct?
options: X has the higher NPS because it has more promoters
Y has the higher NPS because it has fewer detractors
Both have NPS +40, but X has four times the detractor share to address
NPS cannot be calculated without first knowing the exact share of passives in each company
quiz.explanation: X: 60 − 20 = +40. Y: 45 − 5 = +40. Equal scores can hide very different distributions; X has four times the detractor share. Passives are simply the remainder (20% and 50%) and are not needed for the calculation.

quiz.question: A telecom wants to know whether the redesign of its SIM replacement process made it easier for customers. Which measure is most directly suited?
options: A twice-yearly relationship NPS survey
A transactional CES question asked soon after a SIM replacement
The number of new SIM sales
Average handling time in the call centre
quiz.explanation: Ease of a specific process is best measured by a transactional effort question asked right after the experience. Relationship NPS is too broad and slow; SIM sales and AHT do not measure ease for the customer.

quiz.question: At the end of a call, an agent says: "You will receive a short survey; if you give me 10, it really helps my evaluation." What is the main problem?
options: The agent should mention the survey only in English
The agent should ask for a 9 rather than a 10, so that the request sounds more realistic
Surveys should never be mentioned to customers
It is survey begging, which inflates scores and makes the data unreliable
quiz.explanation: Asking for a specific score biases responses and is a classic form of metric gaming. Telling customers a survey is coming can be acceptable; asking for a particular score is not, whatever the number.

quiz.question: Which activity is part of closing the outer loop rather than the inner loop?
options: Grouping root causes from detractor calls and assigning a cross-functional owner
Calling a detractor within two working days to understand the issue and agree a fix
Waiving a fee for a customer who complained
Thanking a customer for their feedback by SMS
quiz.explanation: The outer loop deals with patterns and root causes across many customers, assigning owners and actions. Calling a detractor, fixing their issue and thanking them are inner-loop activities with individual customers.

quiz.question: A contact centre manager sets a strict target to cut average handling time by 20%. Which companion metric would best reveal whether this is harming customers?
options: Number of agents on shift
Call abandonment rate
Repeat contacts on the same issue within 7 days (FCR)
Number of calls answered per hour
quiz.explanation: If agents rush to cut handling time, issues go unresolved and customers call back. FCR/repeat contact catches that directly. Calls per hour moves with AHT and would hide the harm; abandonment and staffing do not show resolution quality.

sessions.title: Designing and Leading a CX Culture
sessions.summary: Turn CX from a project into a way of working: set service standards, improve employee experience, empower staff within guardrails, manage complaints to the standard regulators expect, improve continuously and build a CX strategy and business case leaders will fund.
objectives: Write service standards that are specific, observable and grounded in customer needs
Explain the link between employee experience, empowerment and customer experience
Describe complaint-management expectations and escalation routes in regulated sectors in Pakistan
Apply continuous improvement cycles and pilots to CX changes
Build a CX strategy and a quantified business case

cards.title: Service standards that actually guide behaviour
cards.body:
A brand promise such as "we put customers first" means little to a teller at 3 pm on salary day. **Service standards** turn the promise into concrete behaviours and outcomes that staff can deliver and managers can check.

**Good standards are:**

- **Derived from customer needs.** Start with what customers value at each moment of truth (from Session 2 research), not with what is easy to measure.
- **Specific and observable.** "Greet every customer within 30 seconds of reaching the counter, even if you are busy" can be checked. "Be friendly" cannot.
- **Realistic.** A standard that cannot be met with current staffing teaches people to ignore standards.
- **Few.** Five to ten core standards per channel are remembered; fifty are not.
- **Owned and measured.** Each standard has a way of being checked: mystery shopping, call quality review, system data or customer feedback.

**Examples by type:**

| Type | Example standard |
|---|---|
| Behaviour | Use the customer's name and a respectful title at least once |
| Timeliness | Reply to WhatsApp messages within 15 minutes during service hours |
| Accuracy | Quote all fees and charges before the customer signs |
| Ownership | The person who receives a complaint gives their name and owns it until handover is confirmed |
| Closing | Confirm the next step, the timeline and the reference number at the end of every interaction |

**Standards versus scripts.** Standards define *what* must happen; they should leave room for *how*. Rigid word-for-word scripts often sound robotic and fail when the conversation does not follow the script. Use scripts only where precise wording is required, such as regulatory disclosures and security checks.

Standards should be reviewed at least yearly against customer feedback and changed when customer expectations change.

cards.title: Standards for a private hospital's front desk
cards.body:
A private hospital in Islamabad found that patient complaints focused on the front desk and billing rather than on medical care. Interviews revealed what patients and families valued most: knowing how long they would wait, being treated with dignity when anxious, and avoiding billing surprises at discharge.

The patient experience manager, Dr Rabia Saleem, worked with front-desk staff to write seven standards, including:

1. Greet every patient or family member within 30 seconds, standing if seated.
2. Tell every outpatient the expected waiting time and update them if it changes by more than 15 minutes.
3. Offer a seat and water to elderly patients and those who are visibly unwell.
4. Give inpatient families a written cost estimate within 24 hours of admission, explained in Urdu or English as preferred, and update it if the estimate changes significantly.
5. Never discuss a patient's condition or bill where others can hear.

**How they made it stick:**

- Staff helped write the standards, so they were realistic and owned.
- A monthly mystery-shopping visit and a short SMS survey measured each standard.
- Team leads discussed one standard per week in a ten-minute huddle, sharing a real example of it done well.
- Billing systems were changed so that estimates could actually be produced within 24 hours. Without that change, standard 4 would have been impossible.

Within six months, complaints about billing surprises had roughly halved. The key lesson: standard 4 succeeded because the hospital fixed the backstage process that the standard depended on.

cards.title: Employee experience drives customer experience
cards.body:
Customers experience what employees are able to deliver. A well-known management model, often called the **service-profit chain**, links the two: capable, supported and fairly treated employees deliver better service, better service builds customer loyalty, and loyalty drives growth and profit. Research supports the general link, though the strength varies by industry.

**What shapes employee experience in service roles:**

- **Tools that work.** Slow systems, multiple logins and missing information frustrate staff and customers alike.
- **Authority to help.** Few things demoralise staff more than seeing what the customer needs and not being allowed to do it.
- **Reasonable workload.** Chronic understaffing on predictable peaks (start of month, before Eid) burns people out.
- **Fair, sensible targets.** Targets that conflict with good service, such as cross-selling quotas on every call, push staff into behaviour they know customers dislike.
- **Support after hard interactions.** Contact-centre agents may face many angry callers each day. Short breaks after abusive calls and supervisor debriefs matter.
- **Recognition.** Specific praise for real customer outcomes, shared publicly, reinforces the right behaviour.
- **Being heard.** Frontline staff know where processes break. Organisations that ask them, act on their ideas and say so build engagement and better CX at the same time.

**Practical measures:** track employee engagement or eNPS alongside customer metrics; analyse attrition by team; and include frontline staff in journey mapping and redesign.

In Pakistan's contact-centre and retail sectors, attrition is often high. Each departure takes knowledge with it and forces new staff to learn on live customers. Reducing avoidable attrition is a CX investment.

cards.question: A bank's branch staff must offer a credit card to every walk-in customer to meet daily targets. Customers complain of being pushed, and staff say they are embarrassed. What is the root issue from a CX culture perspective?
options: Staff need sales training to make the offer more smoothly
Customers in Pakistan dislike credit cards
Incentives and targets conflict with good service, damaging both employee and customer experience
The credit card product is poorly designed
cards.explanation: The target forces an offer regardless of the customer's need, which creates pressure for both sides. Better sales technique cannot fix a target that ignores context. Nothing in the case points to product design or general dislike of cards.

cards.title: Empowerment within guardrails
cards.body:
**Empowerment** means giving staff the authority, information and confidence to solve customer problems without unnecessary escalation. It is the main enabler of fast service recovery and first-contact resolution.

Empowerment is not "do whatever you like". It works best with clear **guardrails**:

- **Defined decision rights.** For example: agents may waive late fees up to PKR 1,000, branch managers up to PKR 5,000, and anything above goes to the regional head.
- **Principles for judgement.** "Restore the customer to where they would have been if we had not failed; add a gesture when the inconvenience was significant."
- **Logging and review.** Every discretionary action is recorded, and patterns are reviewed for consistency and misuse.
- **Non-negotiables.** Regulatory, credit and security rules (KYC, AML checks, credit decisions, data privacy) are not open to frontline discretion.

**Empowerment also requires:**

- **Information**: access to the customer's history and case status.
- **Skills**: training in judgement, not just procedure, using real cases.
- **Psychological safety**: staff must trust that a reasonable decision made in good faith will be supported, even if a manager would have chosen differently. If one mistake leads to a show-cause notice, staff will escalate everything.

**A simple approach for leaders** is to look at what is most often escalated. If a type of request is escalated hundreds of times a month and almost always approved, the approval adds delay but little control. Push that decision down, with limits and audit.

Empowered staff fix problems faster, and customers notice that the person in front of them can actually help. That feeling of being in capable hands is a large part of trust.

cards.title: Empowering telecom franchise staff
cards.body:
A telecom operator's franchises in southern Punjab escalated every billing dispute to the central back office, which took an average of five working days to respond. Analysis of one quarter showed:

- About 9,000 disputes were escalated.
- Around 85% were for amounts under PKR 800.
- Around 92% of those small disputes were resolved in the customer's favour.

The back office was spending most of its effort approving small credits it would almost always approve anyway, and customers were making repeat visits to franchises to check progress.

**The change:** franchise supervisors received authority to credit disputed amounts up to PKR 800 on the spot, after checking usage records on a new screen. Each credit required a reason code. A monthly report flagged supervisors whose credit rates were far above or below the average.

**Results after three months:**

- Most small disputes were resolved during the first visit.
- Repeat visits about billing disputes fell substantially.
- The back office could focus on complex and high-value disputes, and its own response time improved.
- Total value credited rose only slightly, because the customers who would have received credits after five days now received them on the spot.
- Two supervisors with unusual patterns were reviewed; one had misunderstood the reason codes and was retrained.

The operator gained speed and customer goodwill with very little added financial risk, because the guardrails (limit, data, reason code and monitoring) were designed first.

cards.title: Complaint management in regulated sectors
cards.body:
In banking, insurance, telecom and other regulated sectors, complaint handling is not only good practice; regulators expect it, and they treat poor complaint handling as a conduct issue.

**What regulators generally expect from banks in Pakistan.** The State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) has issued instructions on consumer grievance handling and on fair treatment of customers. In broad terms, banks are expected to:

- Maintain a **dedicated complaint-handling function** with senior oversight and clear accountability.
- Make complaint channels **easy to find and use**, in branches, on websites, by phone and through digital channels, and publicise them.
- **Acknowledge** complaints promptly with a reference number and **resolve them within set timelines**, keeping the customer informed.
- Give the customer a **clear, reasoned response** and inform them of **further escalation options** if they are not satisfied.
- **Record and analyse** complaints for root causes and report to senior management and the board.
- Treat customers fairly throughout, with no penalty for complaining.

Specific timelines, reporting formats and requirements change from time to time, so **always check the latest SBP circulars and your bank's own policy** rather than relying on memory.

**External escalation routes.** If a customer is not satisfied with the bank's final response, or the bank does not respond within the allowed time, the customer can take the complaint to the **Banking Mohtasib Pakistan**, an independent ombudsman that handles banking complaints free of charge, subject to its rules on eligibility and timing. Customers can also lodge complaints with SBP through its own complaint channel. Other sectors have their own routes: for example, insurance complaints can go to the **Federal Insurance Ombudsman**, and telecom customers can complain to the **Pakistan Telecommunication Authority** after approaching the operator.

**Why it matters for CX:** complaints that reach an ombudsman are almost always cases where the organisation's own process failed. Good internal handling is cheaper, faster and better for trust.

cards.title: A complaint that reached the Mohtasib
cards.body:
Mr Javed Iqbal, a small trader in Sargodha, noticed that an annual fee had been charged twice on his debit card. He complained at his branch and was told it would be checked. No reference number was given. Two weeks later he called the helpline, which had no record of the branch complaint and opened a new one. The response, three weeks after that, was a one-line email in English saying the charge was "as per schedule of charges".

Mr Iqbal did not understand the reply and was not told how to escalate. A relative helped him file a complaint with the Banking Mohtasib. During the process the bank re-examined the case, found the fee had indeed been charged twice due to a system error affecting a batch of cards, and reversed it.

**The bank's review found failures at every step:**

- The branch did not log the complaint or give a reference, contrary to the bank's own policy.
- Channels did not share complaint records.
- The investigator checked the fee schedule but not the transaction history.
- The reply was unclear, not in the customer's preferred language, and did not mention escalation options.
- Nobody asked whether other customers were affected.

**Actions taken:**

- Every complaint, in every channel, is now logged in one system with an immediate reference by SMS.
- Final responses must explain the reasoning in plain language, in Urdu or English as preferred, and state the escalation route.
- Complaints that suggest a system error trigger a check of similar accounts. In this case, several hundred other cardholders received automatic refunds.

A few hundred rupees became a regulatory, reputational and operational lesson.

cards.question: A bank customer is unhappy with the bank's final written reply to her complaint about a disputed charge. What is the most appropriate information for the bank's reply to have included?
options: A statement that the bank's decision is final and cannot be challenged
Advice to post her complaint on social media to get attention
The bank's reasoning in plain language and the external escalation options, such as the Banking Mohtasib
A request to visit the branch to discuss the complaint again
cards.explanation: Banks are expected to give a reasoned response and to inform customers of further escalation routes, such as the Banking Mohtasib. Claiming the decision cannot be challenged is misleading; social media is not a formal route; another branch visit adds effort without offering a path.

cards.title: Continuous improvement: small cycles, real evidence
cards.body:
CX culture is visible in how an organisation improves, not in its posters. Mature organisations treat improvement as a routine, not a campaign.

**The Plan-Do-Check-Act (PDCA) cycle:**

1. **Plan:** define the problem with data, find the root cause and design a change with a clear hypothesis: "If we send a status SMS on day 3, calls asking about loan status will fall by a third."
2. **Do:** test it on a small scale, such as a few branches, one region or a share of customers.
3. **Check:** compare results with a **control group** that did not receive the change, over a long enough period.
4. **Act:** scale what works, adjust what partly works, and stop what does not.

**Why pilots and controls matter:** many things change at once in a business: seasons, campaigns, staffing, competitor moves. Without a control group, it is easy to credit a CX change with an improvement that would have happened anyway, or to drop a good idea because of an unrelated dip.

**Habits of continuous-improvement cultures:**

- **Daily or weekly huddles** where teams review a few customer comments and one improvement idea.
- **Visible boards** tracking top pain points, owners and status.
- **Frontline idea schemes** where suggestions get a response within a set time.
- **Celebrating removed problems**, not only high scores: "We eliminated 20,000 calls a month about card PINs."
- **Learning reviews** after major failures that ask what in the system allowed the failure, rather than who to blame.

Leaders set the tone. When a senior manager asks "what did customers tell us this week and what are we doing about it?" in every review meeting, the organisation learns that CX is real work.

cards.title: CX strategy and the business case
cards.body:
A **CX strategy** answers four questions:

1. **What experience do we want to be known for?** A short, specific ambition linked to the brand and to what target customers value, for example "the easiest bank for small traders to do business with".
2. **Which journeys matter most?** Choose a handful of priority journeys based on value at stake and pain today.
3. **How will we organise?** Governance (a senior CX forum), clear journey owners across functions, a VoC programme and a measurement framework.
4. **How will we fund and sequence it?** Quick wins that build credibility, plus structural fixes in processes, systems and policies.

**Building the business case.** Finance teams respond to rupees, assumptions and evidence. Typical value sources:

- **Retention:** reduced churn × CLV (Session 1).
- **Failure demand reduction:** contacts caused by failures ("where is my card?", "why is my bill wrong?") cost money. Fewer such contacts × cost per contact = savings.
- **Cost to serve:** moving suitable interactions to effective self-service.
- **Revenue growth:** more products per customer, referrals and share of wallet.
- **Risk reduction:** fewer regulatory complaints, ombudsman cases and penalties.

**Credibility rules:**

- Use your own data where possible; label assumptions clearly and keep them conservative.
- Show a range (low, expected, high) rather than a single heroic number.
- Include all costs: technology, training, process change and staff time.
- Do not double-count; the same call saved should not appear as both a cost saving and a retention gain.
- Commit to a measurement plan, ideally with a pilot and control group.

A modest, well-evidenced case that is delivered builds more credibility for the next one than an ambitious case that is not.

cards.title: A business case built on failure demand
cards.body:
Kamran Shah, CX manager at an electricity distribution company, wants to redesign the monthly bill and the billing-query journey.

**Baseline data (from the company's own systems):**

- The contact centre handles 1.2 million calls a year.
- Call coding shows 30% are billing queries: 360,000 calls.
- The fully loaded cost per call is PKR 120.

**Expected impact (from a three-month pilot in one circle with a control circle):** billing calls in the pilot fell by 40% compared with the control. Kamran uses **35%** company-wide as a conservative estimate.

**Annual savings from reduced failure demand:**

- 360,000 × 35% = 126,000 fewer calls
- 126,000 × PKR 120 = **PKR 15.12 million a year**

**Costs:**

- Bill redesign and printing changes: PKR 6 million (one-off)
- System changes for clearer bill explanations: PKR 9 million (one-off)
- Training and communication: PKR 3 million (one-off)
- **Total one-off cost: PKR 18 million**

**Payback:** 18 ÷ 15.12 ≈ **1.2 years** on call savings alone.

Kamran also lists, but does not add to the core numbers, the likely reduction in walk-in visits to customer service centres and in formal complaints, presenting these as upside. He shows a low case (25% reduction, payback about 1.7 years) and a high case (40%, about 1.0 years).

The board approves the project because the evidence came from a controlled pilot, the assumptions were conservative and the costs were complete.

cards.title: Avoid CX theatre
cards.body: Signs that CX has become theatre: a "customer week" with balloons but no process changes; dashboards reviewed monthly with no decisions recorded; a CX team with no authority over any journey; and awards for scores that customers' behaviour does not confirm. The test of a CX culture is simple: **what changed for customers this quarter, and how do we know?**

cards.question: A CX business case claims savings of PKR 20 million from fewer billing calls and adds a further PKR 20 million retention benefit calculated from the same customers no longer needing to call. What is the main flaw?
options: Retention benefits should never be included in a CX business case
The case risks double-counting the same improvement, which undermines credibility with finance
The savings should be calculated per branch rather than company-wide
Call savings are not a valid source of value
cards.explanation: Retention and failure-demand savings can both be valid, but counting the same effect twice inflates the case. Finance teams will spot it and distrust the rest. Retention benefits are legitimate when estimated separately from evidence.

cards.title: Take-aways from the Citadel of Lanterns
items: Service standards should be few, specific, observable, realistic and grounded in customer needs, with backstage processes able to support them.
Employee experience drives customer experience: tools, workload, fair targets, support and recognition all matter.
Empower staff with clear decision rights, information, skills and psychological safety, inside regulatory and risk guardrails.
Regulated complaint handling means easy access, references, timelines, reasoned responses, escalation information and root-cause analysis; check current regulatory instructions.
Banking Mohtasib, the Federal Insurance Ombudsman and sector regulators are external escalation routes when internal handling fails.
Improve through PDCA cycles and controlled pilots; celebrate problems removed, not just scores.
A credible CX business case uses own data, conservative ranges, complete costs, no double-counting and a measurement plan.

cards.prompt: If you had to present one CX improvement to your leadership next month, which journey would you choose, what value sources would you quantify, and what pilot would prove it works?

quiz.question: Which of the following is the best-written service standard?
options: Always provide excellent and friendly service
Confirm the next step, timeline and reference number at the end of every customer interaction
Make every customer feel like family
Do your best to resolve complaints quickly
quiz.explanation: Option B is specific, observable and measurable, and links to what customers value. The others express good intentions but cannot be consistently checked or coached.

quiz.question: A retailer introduces a standard: "All home-delivery customers receive a two-hour delivery window by SMS the evening before." After two months, the standard is met for only 40% of deliveries, and staff have started ignoring it. What is the most likely cause?
options: Customers do not want delivery windows
The standard is not specific enough for staff to know exactly what is expected of them
Staff were not told about the standard
Backstage dispatch cannot yet produce two-hour windows reliably
quiz.explanation: The standard is specific and clearly communicated, but staff cannot meet it without a supporting process. Standards that the system cannot deliver teach staff to ignore standards. Fix the backstage capability or adjust the standard.

quiz.question: Which statement best reflects the service-profit chain idea?
options: Profit should be maximised first, so that the company can afford to pay employees more
Customer loyalty is determined mainly by price
Supported, capable employees give better service, which builds loyalty and profit
Employee satisfaction and customer satisfaction are unrelated
quiz.explanation: The model links internal service quality and employee experience to service value, loyalty and profit. It does not claim price is the main driver, and it explicitly connects employee and customer outcomes.

quiz.question: Data shows that agents escalate around 3,000 requests a month to waive SMS-alert charges below PKR 300, and supervisors approve 97% of them, usually after a 30-minute delay. What is the best leadership action?
options: Let agents waive charges up to a limit, with reason codes and monitoring
Stop all waivers to remove the workload
Hire additional supervisors so that each approval takes five minutes rather than thirty
Ask customers to submit waiver requests in writing
quiz.explanation: When nearly all escalations are approved, the approval step adds delay and cost but little control. Empowerment with limits, reason codes and monitoring keeps risk managed while speeding resolution. The other options add cost or effort.

quiz.question: A branch officer gave a PKR 1,500 goodwill waiver, within her authority, to a customer whose card was wrongly blocked abroad. Her manager publicly criticises her, saying he would have offered less. What is the likely effect on CX culture?
options: Staff will make more consistent decisions
Staff lose psychological safety and start escalating decisions they are allowed to make
Customers will receive larger waivers in future
There will be no effect on staff, because the waiver was within policy and the customer was retained
quiz.explanation: Empowerment depends on staff trusting that reasonable decisions within their authority will be supported. Public criticism teaches them to escalate everything, which slows recovery. Coaching privately on judgement would have been appropriate.

quiz.question: Which of the following is generally expected of a bank's complaint-handling process in Pakistan?
options: Complaints may be resolved informally and left unrecorded when the customer seems satisfied with the outcome
Complaints should be accepted only in writing at the branch where the account is held
Customers should be told that the bank's decision is final
Acknowledge with a reference, resolve within set timelines, give reasons and explain escalation options
quiz.explanation: Regulatory expectations for banks broadly include acknowledgement with a reference, timely resolution, reasoned responses and information on further escalation such as the Banking Mohtasib. Unrecorded complaints, restricting channels and claiming finality all conflict with these expectations.

quiz.question: A bank's complaint unit notices three complaints in one week about the same unexplained card fee. What should it do beyond resolving the three cases?
options: Wait a few more weeks to see whether more customers complain before starting any investigation
Ask the three customers not to discuss the issue publicly
Check whether a systemic error affects others and correct all affected accounts
Refund the three customers and close the matter
quiz.explanation: Clusters of similar complaints often signal a systemic issue. Fair treatment requires checking for other affected customers and correcting their accounts proactively, not only refunding those who complained. Silencing customers is clearly inappropriate.

quiz.question: A bank pilots a new loan-status SMS in five branches. Calls about loan status from those branches fall 25% over two months. In the same period, calls about loan status from all other branches fall 20% due to a seasonal dip. What is the best estimate of the pilot's effect?
options: A small extra effect of roughly 5 points beyond the seasonal fall, to be confirmed
A 25% reduction, which can be used directly in the business case for a network-wide rollout
No effect at all, so the SMS should be stopped
A 45% reduction, combining both figures
quiz.explanation: The control branches show that most of the fall was seasonal. The SMS adds only about 5 points (strictly, 25% vs 20% is roughly a 6% relative difference). It may still be worthwhile, but needs confirmation over a longer period. Using 25% ignores the control; adding figures is wrong.

quiz.question: A contact centre handles 800,000 calls a year; 25% are "where is my order" calls. A tracking feature is expected to cut those calls by 40%. The cost per call is PKR 100 and the feature costs PKR 12 million one-off. What is the approximate payback period on call savings alone?
options: About 6 months
1.5 years
About 3 years
About 8 months
quiz.explanation: 800,000 × 25% = 200,000 calls; × 40% = 80,000 fewer calls; × PKR 100 = PKR 8 million a year. Payback = 12 ÷ 8 = 1.5 years. About 8 months comes from inverting the ratio (8 ÷ 12 ≈ 0.67 years); 3 years would follow only if calls fell by 20% instead of 40%.

quiz.question: A customer's complaint about a wrongly declined insurance claim has received a final response from the insurer that she considers unfair. Which escalation route is most appropriate?
options: The Banking Mohtasib
The Pakistan Telecommunication Authority
A consumer survey run by the insurer
The Federal Insurance Ombudsman
quiz.explanation: Insurance complaints that are not resolved by the insurer can be taken to the Federal Insurance Ombudsman. The Banking Mohtasib handles banking complaints and PTA handles telecom. A survey is not an escalation route.

bank.question: A microfinance bank earns an average annual profit of PKR 9,000 per active borrower and retains 70% of borrowers each year. Using the simple estimate CLV ≈ annual profit × (1 ÷ churn), what is the approximate lifetime value of a borrower?
bank.explanation: Churn = 1 − 0.70 = 0.30, so expected relationship ≈ 1 ÷ 0.30 ≈ 3.33 years. CLV ≈ 9,000 × 3.33 = PKR 30,000. PKR 27,000 rounds the relationship down to 3 years; PKR 12,857 divides by retention; PKR 6,300 multiplies by retention.

bank.question: A regional bank has 50,000 retail customers, each producing PKR 10,000 annual profit. A CX programme is expected to lift retention from 75% to 80%. Using CLV ≈ annual profit ÷ churn, roughly how much total lifetime value does the improvement add across the base?
options: PKR 500 million
PKR 25 million
PKR 2.5 billion
PKR 125 million
bank.explanation: CLV rises from 10,000 ÷ 0.25 = 40,000 to 10,000 ÷ 0.20 = 50,000, a gain of PKR 10,000 per customer. × 50,000 customers = PKR 500 million. PKR 2.5 billion is the new total CLV, not the gain; PKR 25 million applies the 5-point change to one year's profit.

bank.question: At a strategy meeting, a telecom's chief operating officer says: "CX is the contact centre's responsibility; their scores are excellent, so we are fine." Meanwhile complaints about billing errors and network drops are rising. Which reply best reflects CX thinking?
options: Agree, and ask the contact centre to absorb the higher complaint volumes by recruiting more agents
Agree, but add a CSAT survey for billing calls to confirm the scores
Disagree, and move the contact centre under the marketing department
Disagree: billing and the network shape experience, so CX needs shared, top-led ownership
bank.explanation: Experience is created by every function; billing systems and the network are owned outside the contact centre. Good agent scores cannot remove the causes. Extra staff or extra surveys treat symptoms, and moving reporting lines does not create shared ownership.

bank.question: A bank's retention rate is 94%, but only 1.2 products are held per customer, relationship NPS is −15, and most accounts are salary accounts opened through employers. A large employer is considering moving its payroll to a digital bank. What is the most accurate interpretation?
options: High retention proves strong loyalty, so losing the employer's payroll would affect few customers
Much of the retention is captive, so the base is exposed if payroll moves
Low product holding shows customers are price-sensitive, so fees should be cut
A negative NPS is normal for banks and can be ignored if retention is high
bank.explanation: High retention combined with low share of wallet and negative NPS signals captive behaviour rather than attitudinal loyalty. When the employer changes payroll bank, many customers may leave with it. Low product holding alone does not prove price sensitivity.

bank.question: A health insurer's data shows that members whose first claim took over 30 days to settle lapse at renewal at 45%, compared with 15% for members whose first claim was settled within 10 days. With budget for one improvement, which should it prioritise?
options: Speeding up and communicating the first-claim journey
A redesigned welcome pack for new members
Discounts at renewal for all members
A new advertising campaign about claim speed
bank.explanation: The first claim is a moment of truth with a clear, large link to lapse behaviour. Fixing it addresses the cause. Renewal discounts cost money without fixing the experience, and advertising claim speed before improving it raises expectations the insurer cannot meet.

bank.question: Hospital discharge takes about four hours. Families report that the worst moment is being called to the billing counter and told, in front of others, about unexpected charges. Which change is likely to improve families' memory of the stay most for the least cost?
options: Reduce discharge time from four hours to three and a half by adding a clerk
Send a satisfaction survey by SMS within one hour of discharge
Share cost updates privately each day and review the final bill privately
Install a television and free tea in the discharge lounge
bank.explanation: The peak-end effect means the humiliating billing surprise (a negative peak that also forms the ending) dominates memory. Removing the surprise and handling the ending privately addresses both. A modest time cut costs more and changes memory less; a survey only measures.

bank.question: An insurer earns PKR 6,000 annual profit per policyholder. Retention improves from 85% to 88%. By roughly how much does the simple CLV estimate per policyholder rise?
options: About PKR 1,200
About PKR 18,000
About PKR 2,000
About PKR 10,000
bank.explanation: CLV moves from 6,000 ÷ 0.15 = 40,000 to 6,000 ÷ 0.12 = 50,000, an increase of about PKR 10,000. PKR 1,200 applies the 3-point change to 40,000; PKR 2,000 and PKR 18,000 do not follow from the formula. Note that a three-point retention gain increases CLV by 25%.

bank.question: A new credit card arrives on time and works correctly, but activation requires a 12-minute call with long security questions and two transfers. Many customers rate the experience poorly. Which idea best explains this?
options: Customers only value speed of delivery
High effort produces negative emotion even when the outcome is correct
Customers judge experiences by the average of all steps
The product itself must be poor
bank.explanation: The outcome is fine, but effort (time, repetition, transfers) drives frustration and shapes the memory. Averaging is not how memory works, and nothing suggests the product is poor.

bank.question: Which situation is the clearest example of a moment of decision?
options: A customer's first visit to a newly opened branch
A customer reporting a stolen phone late at night and asking to block the SIM
A customer weighing a rival's offer as her car insurance renewal nears
A customer receiving a monthly account statement
bank.explanation: A renewal with a competing offer is a stay-or-leave point where the accumulated experience turns into a choice. A first visit is a first impression; a stolen phone is a moment of need; a routine statement is low-stakes.

bank.question: A bank's CX lead reviews: courtesy scores for call-centre agents at 92%; complaints about card delivery up 40%; relationship NPS down 9 points; retention flat at 93%, driven by payroll accounts. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Courtesy is masking a journey failure; retention may be captive, so card delivery needs a cross-functional owner
Since retention is flat, the NPS decline is most likely survey noise and does not need action in this financial year
The card complaints show agents are failing to explain delivery times, so the priority is script training
Customers are less loyal in general, so the bank should increase acquisition spending to offset future losses
bank.explanation: The evidence points to a journey problem (card delivery) outside the call centre, with flat retention likely supported by captive payroll customers. A 9-point drop alongside rising complaints is unlikely to be noise; script training treats a symptom; acquisition spend ignores the cause.

bank.question: A digital bank sees that 60% of users who start a personal-loan application in the app abandon it at the income-verification step. Which VoC approach will best explain why?
options: A twice-yearly relationship NPS survey of all customers
Funnel analytics on the step, combined with observed usability sessions with target users
A focus group of senior managers who use the app
Counting app-store reviews that mention loans
bank.explanation: Behavioural data locates the drop-off precisely, and watching real users attempt the step reveals why. A relationship survey is too broad; managers are not representative; review counts show volume but not the cause at that step.

bank.question: A bank wants feedback it can use to coach individual branch teams on service at the counter. Which design is most suitable?
options: A national relationship survey run once a year, with results reported by province and region
A social-listening report on mentions of the bank
Exit interviews with customers who close accounts
A short transactional survey sent automatically after branch visits, linked to the branch
bank.explanation: Coaching needs timely feedback about specific interactions, which transactional surveys linked to the branch provide. Annual relationship surveys are too infrequent and aggregated; social listening and exit interviews cannot be reliably tied to particular teams.

bank.question: A motor insurer currently surveys claimants the day a claim is registered, and scores are high. Complaints about claim delays remain common. What change to survey timing is most appropriate?
options: Survey after settlement, with an optional pulse at registration
Stop surveying claimants because the scores are already high
Survey only the claimants whose claims were approved, since they can comment on the whole process
Move the survey to the renewal date one year later
bank.explanation: At registration nothing has been tested yet, so the survey captures hope rather than experience. Surveying after settlement captures delays and outcomes. Surveying only approved claims biases the sample; waiting a year loses detail.

bank.question: A telecom's marketing team created 11 personas two years ago from internal brainstorming. Product teams say they never use them. What is the best way forward?
options: Add more personal detail, such as hobbies and favourite TV shows, so the personas feel memorable
Replace personas with age and income segments, which are easier to measure
Rebuild a few needs-based personas from research and use them in design reviews
Distribute the existing personas again with a memo asking teams to use them
bank.explanation: Personas fail when they are assumption-based, too numerous and not built into decisions. A few evidence-based, needs-based personas used in design reviews fix all three. More trivia, demographic bands or reminders do not address the causes.

bank.question: A retailer's project team wants to start its journey-mapping workshop by designing the ideal future app experience, since "everyone already knows the current problems". What is the strongest advice?
options: Proceed as planned, because designing the future state is the most valuable part of the work
Ask the app vendor to propose the future state instead
Skip mapping and run an NPS survey first
Map the current state with customer evidence first, so the redesign targets real pain
bank.explanation: Assumed knowledge of current problems is often wrong or incomplete. An evidence-based current-state map shows where effort and emotion actually peak. A vendor proposal or an NPS score alone cannot locate pain points within the journey.

bank.question: An electricity distributor investigates billing complaints using the five whys: bills are wrong → readings are estimated → readers cannot access meters inside locked homes → visits happen during working hours when no one is home → ? Which next answer is the most useful root cause to act on?
options: Customers are rarely at home and should stay in more
There is no way for customers to book a reading visit or submit their own verified reading
Meter readers are lazy and need disciplinary action
Estimated billing is permitted under the regulations, so there is no real problem here to solve
bank.explanation: A useful root cause is systemic, within the company's control and fixable with an owner, such as booking or self-submitted readings. Blaming customers or readers stops the analysis too early, and the permissibility of estimates does not remove the complaints.

bank.question: In a blueprint of branch account opening, documents are scanned at the branch, but the original forms are couriered once a day to central operations, which verifies them before activation. Accounts take three days to activate. Which of these is best described as a wait point?
options: Forms waiting for the daily courier batch before central verification can begin
The teller checking the customer's original CNIC
Central operations re-typing form data into the core system
The welcome letter the customer receives
bank.explanation: A wait point is where work or the customer sits idle in a queue or batch. Re-typing data is a fail point (error-prone), the CNIC check is a frontstage action, and the welcome letter is physical evidence.

bank.question: A card unit's monthly contacts are: PIN reset 3,200; card delivery status 2,600; app login 1,400; fee queries 500; other 300. What share of all contacts do the top two reasons represent?
bank.explanation: Total = 8,000. PIN reset + card delivery = 5,800. 5,800 ÷ 8,000 = 72.5%. 90% is the share of the top three. Pareto analysis shows that fixing these two reasons would address most contact volume.

bank.question: A journey map shows customers are anxious after depositing a cheque because the app shows nothing for a day. The service blueprint reveals that clearing is completed the same day, but the app shows transactions only after an overnight posting batch. What is the most effective fix?
options: Train agents to reassure customers who call about deposited cheques
Speed up the clearing process so that every cheque is cleared before noon on the same day
Add a note on the deposit slip asking customers to be patient
Show the backstage status (received, in clearing, cleared) in the app in near real time
bank.explanation: The blueprint shows the delay is in visibility, not processing. Exposing backstage status removes the anxiety at its source. Faster clearing would not help because the app still updates overnight; reassuring callers and slip notes treat symptoms.

bank.question: In a service blueprint, what does the line of visibility separate?
options: Customer actions from physical evidence
Frontstage actions the customer sees from backstage actions they do not see
Support processes from IT systems
Online channels from offline channels
bank.explanation: The line of visibility divides what the customer can see (frontstage) from what happens out of sight (backstage and support). It is not a channel boundary, and it does not split customer actions from physical evidence.

bank.question: An agent tells a customer: "I can't process your address change without the signed form." Which rewording best applies positive, action-focused language while staying accurate?
options: "Once I have the signed form, I can update it the same day. Shall I send it on WhatsApp?"
"Don't worry, I will update your address now and you can send the signed form whenever convenient."
"Unfortunately, that's the policy and I have no choice."
"You should have brought the form with you."
bank.explanation: Option A leads with what can be done, gives a clear timeline and makes the next step easy, without breaking the rule. Option B promises to bypass a control; C is negative and policy-focused; D blames the customer.

bank.question: A quality reviewer notices an agent spent 35 minutes on a call repeatedly reassuring a customer about a failed transfer, with warm language throughout, but never traced the transfer. The customer called again the next day. What is the most useful coaching point?
options: Empathy should be dropped in favour of a strict script
The agent should have transferred the call to a supervisor at once
Empathy should lead quickly to action; warmth without resolution adds effort
The call was handled well, because the customer was treated warmly and patiently throughout
bank.explanation: Empathy is valuable when it leads the customer into a solution. Here it replaced resolution, causing a repeat contact. Dropping empathy goes too far, an immediate transfer adds effort, and warmth alone did not meet the customer's need.

bank.question: A customer arrives upset about a blocked account. Before the customer finishes speaking, the officer explains the bank's dormancy policy in detail. Which ASAAN step has been skipped or rushed?
options: Agree and act
Acknowledge
Notify and follow through
Apologise appropriately
bank.explanation: Acknowledge means listening without interrupting and recognising the feeling before explaining or defending. Jumping to policy skips it and usually escalates frustration. The later steps cannot work well until the customer feels heard.

bank.question: A well-known local businessman insists a relationship officer open an account for his nephew today without the required identity documents, saying, "Do you know who I am? Your regional head is my friend." What is the best response?
options: Open the account and collect documents next week, given his importance
Call the regional head and ask for permission to open the account now and collect documents later
Politely refuse and ask him to leave the branch
Stay courteous, explain the rule cannot be waived, and offer the fastest compliant route
bank.explanation: Identity requirements are non-negotiable, whoever the customer is. Treating him with high courtesy while applying the same rule, and offering the quickest compliant path, protects both the customer relationship and the bank. Asking the regional head to bypass the rule is still a breach.

bank.question: A bank debited a trader's PKR 40,000 payment twice. As a result, his cheque to a supplier bounced, he paid a bounce charge and was embarrassed with his supplier. Which recovery is most appropriate?
options: Reverse the duplicate debit and send a standard apology SMS
Reverse the duplicate debit and offer a free cheque book
Reverse it, refund the bounce charge, give a letter admitting the error, apologise and fix the cause
Ask the trader to submit a formal written complaint so the case can be investigated within the usual timeline
bank.explanation: Recovery should restore the customer fully, including knock-on costs, and repair reputational harm, here with a letter for the supplier, plus a sincere apology and a root-cause fix. Reversing the debit alone leaves him out of pocket and embarrassed; making him file formally delays an obvious remedy.

bank.question: An e-commerce company refunded a customer in full within 24 hours for a damaged mixer grinder. However, the agent said on the call, "Customers like you always find something to complain about." The customer still posted an angry review. Which fairness dimension failed?
options: Fair treatment
Fair outcome
Fair process
None, because the refund was full and fast
bank.explanation: The outcome (full refund) and process (24 hours) were fair, but the customer was treated with disrespect. Customers judge interpersonal treatment separately, and disrespect alone can turn a well-resolved case into a detractor.

bank.question: A customer writes on the company's official WhatsApp: "Mera bill is month double kyun aya hai? Koi batayega?" Brand guidelines allow replies in English, Urdu or Roman Urdu. What is the best approach for the reply?
options: Reply in formal English, because written replies should always be in English
Reply in simple Roman Urdu, matching the customer, without billing jargon
Ask the customer to call the helpline because WhatsApp is not for billing
Send a link to the full tariff document in English
bank.explanation: Following the customer's language and keeping explanations simple reduces effort and misunderstanding, and is within the brand guidelines. Insisting on English or redirecting to another channel adds effort; a tariff document does not answer why this bill doubled.

bank.question: A bank plans to close pension counters at urban branches within three months and require pensioners to use the app, to cut costs. Many pensioners are elderly and some have low literacy. Which approach best balances cost and CX?
options: Proceed as planned; pensioners will adapt once counters close
Cancel the digital plan entirely, since older customers generally cannot use apps safely
Keep counters open indefinitely but stop promoting the app
Phase it: assisted onboarding, simple Urdu guides and a retained assisted route
bank.explanation: Good omnichannel design guides customers to digital where it helps while keeping an assisted route for those excluded. Forcing the change risks hardship and complaints; assuming older customers cannot use apps is a stereotype; abandoning promotion loses the cost and convenience benefits.

bank.question: A woman customer at a busy branch counter hesitates and lowers her voice when asked about a loan for a family medical emergency. What should the officer do?
options: Offer to continue at a private desk, or with a female colleague if she prefers
Ask her to speak up so the details can be recorded correctly
Ask her to return with a male family member
Continue at the counter but speak faster to save her time
bank.explanation: Offering privacy, and a female colleague if preferred, respects dignity and sensitive circumstances without making assumptions. Asking her to speak up publicly, or to bring a male relative, is inappropriate; rushing her does not address the discomfort.

bank.question: A customer is quoted a PKR 0 fee for an inter-bank transfer in the app's fee screen, but the branch charges PKR 200 for the same transfer. The customer complains about being misled. What is the best response?
options: Explain that branch fees legitimately differ from app fees and charge the PKR 200
Refund the PKR 200 only if the customer escalates to a supervisor
Honour the quoted fee, fix the wrong information at source and check for others
Advise the customer to use the app in future and close the case
bank.explanation: The customer relied on information the bank provided. Honouring it, correcting the source and checking for others is fair and fixes the omnichannel inconsistency. Charging regardless or refunding only on escalation rewards persistence rather than fairness.

bank.question: From 1,000 NPS responses: 150 scored 10, 170 scored 9, 200 scored 8, 130 scored 7 and 350 scored 0–6. What is the NPS?
bank.explanation: Promoters = 150 + 170 = 320 (32%). Detractors = 350 (35%). NPS = 32 − 35 = −3. +3 reverses the subtraction; +32 is the promoter share only; −35 is the detractor share only.

bank.question: A telecom has 400 NPS responses: 140 promoters, 120 passives, 140 detractors. A network fix is expected to move 40 detractors to passives, with no other change. What would the new NPS be?
bank.explanation: Current NPS = 35% − 35% = 0. After the change: promoters 140 (35%), detractors 100 (25%), so NPS = 35 − 25 = +10. +20 wrongly treats the moved customers as promoters; +35 ignores detractors.

bank.question: Team A measures effort on a 1–5 scale where 1 means very low effort; its average is 2.1. Team B uses a 1–7 agreement scale for "It was easy to handle my issue"; its average is 5.6. A manager says Team A performs worse because its score is lower. What is correct?
options: The manager is right, because 2.1 is lower than 5.6
Team B is worse because its score is further from the maximum
They cannot be compared directly: the scales and directions differ
Both teams perform the same once both scores are converted to percentages of the maximum
bank.explanation: On Team A's scale lower is better; on Team B's higher is better, and the ranges differ. Both results look fairly positive, but they cannot be ranked against each other. Simple percentage conversion does not fix the different questions and directions.

bank.question: In a month, a contact centre records 12,500 contacts relating to 5,000 unique issues. For 1,100 of those issues, the customer contacted again about the same issue within 7 days. What is FCR using the repeat-contact method?
bank.explanation: Issues resolved at first contact = 5,000 − 1,100 = 3,900. FCR = 3,900 ÷ 5,000 = 78%. 31.2% divides by contacts instead of issues; 22% is the repeat-issue rate.

bank.question: On a 5-point CSAT scale, Branch X's responses are half 5s and half 3s; Branch Y's responses are all 4s. Which statement is correct?
options: Branch X performs better because it has more 5s
Both have an average of 4.0, but top-two-box CSAT is 50% for X and 100% for Y
Both have the same CSAT under every reporting method
Branch Y's top-two-box CSAT is 0% because it has no 5s
bank.explanation: X: (5 + 3) ÷ 2 = 4.0 average; only the 5s count in top-two-box, so 50%. Y: average 4.0; all 4s count, so 100%. This is why reports must state the reporting method and show distributions.

bank.question: A bank sends its branch-experience survey only through an in-app notification. App users are younger and more digitally active than the branch customer base. Scores look strong. What is the main concern?
options: In-app surveys are always less accurate than SMS surveys
The survey should use a 10-point scale
Branch staff should hand out paper surveys instead
The respondents may not represent branch customers, so results can be biased
bank.explanation: The sample excludes many branch customers, such as older or less digital customers, who may have different experiences. That is a coverage bias. The channel is not inherently inaccurate, and staff-handed surveys introduce their own selection bias.
