bank.question: Over six months, a region's CSAT rises from 78% to 95%. In the same period its survey response rate falls from 18% to 6%, complaints from the region to the Banking Mohtasib double, and most branch scores become uniform 5s. What is the best action?
options: Celebrate the region publicly and share its branch practices with other regions as the model to follow
Discount the Mohtasib cases, since they are a small number compared with survey responses
Audit how surveys are triggered, move to automatic sampling and pair CSAT with complaints
Increase CSAT targets for all regions, since 95% has proved achievable
bank.explanation: Falling response rates, uniform top scores and rising external complaints are classic signs of survey steering. An audit, automatic sampling and paired metrics address it. Celebrating or raising targets would reward gaming, and external escalations are a serious signal however few.

bank.question: A branch manager calls a customer who scored 2 on NPS. After hearing the complaint, she asks, "Now that we have discussed it, would you be willing to revise your score?" What is wrong with this?
options: The call should aim to understand and fix; asking to revise the score corrupts the data
Nothing is wrong; revising scores after a resolution makes the survey data more accurate
She should have sent an email instead of calling
Only head-office staff should make inner-loop calls
bank.explanation: The purpose of closing the inner loop is to understand, resolve and learn. Seeking a better score turns the call into gaming and distorts the measure. Phone calls by local managers are an effective way to close the loop.

bank.question: A branch's monthly NPS is based on 25 responses. If one customer moves from detractor to promoter, by how many points does the branch NPS change?
options: 4 points
1 point
2 points
8 points
bank.explanation: One response is 4% of 25. Losing a detractor (−4% detractors) and gaining a promoter (+4% promoters) changes NPS by 8 points. This is why small-sample branch scores should be read as trends, not monthly verdicts.

bank.question: A complaints unit is set a target of closing 95% of complaints within five working days. Which companion metric best guards against cases being closed without a real fix?
options: The number of complaints received per day
The rate of complaints reopened or re-raised by the same customer about the same issue
Average handling time per complaint call, tracked month by month for each team in the unit
The number of staff in the complaints unit
bank.explanation: If cases are closed prematurely, customers come back with the same issue, so reopened complaints reveal it. Volume, handling time and staffing do not show whether closures were genuine.

bank.question: A contact centre requires agents to read a fixed 120-word opening and closing on every call. Customers describe agents as robotic, and some hang up during the opening. What is the best recommendation?
options: Lengthen the script to cover more scenarios
Remove all scripts and guidance completely, and let agents say whatever they feel is right
Set standards for what must happen; keep exact wording only for disclosures and security
Ask agents to read the script faster
bank.explanation: Standards define what must happen and leave room for natural conversation; exact scripts belong where precise wording is required. Longer or faster scripting makes the problem worse; removing all guidance loses consistency.

bank.question: A contact centre in Lahore has annual agent attrition of about 60% and low first-contact resolution. Exit interviews mention slow systems, back-to-back abusive calls and unpredictable rosters at month-end. Which investment is most likely to improve CX?
options: Fix the knowledge tools, plan rosters for known peaks and give support after abusive calls
Hire a larger intake of trainees each quarter to replace leavers faster
Introduce a CSAT-linked retention bonus for agents who stay with the centre for more than a year
Shorten induction training so new agents reach the floor sooner
bank.explanation: The exit interviews name causes that also hurt customers: tools, workload peaks and emotional strain. Fixing them improves both employee and customer experience. More or faster hiring keeps inexperienced agents on live calls; a retention bonus ignores the causes.

bank.question: A bank is designing frontline empowerment limits. Which decision should remain outside frontline discretion?
options: Waiving a PKR 300 late-payment fee after a system delay
Sending a replacement card by courier at no charge after a bank error
Arranging a callback at a time the customer chooses
Accepting a known customer's account update without the required identity verification
bank.explanation: Identity verification is a regulatory and security control, not a service courtesy, so it is a non-negotiable guardrail. Small fee waivers, free replacements after bank errors and flexible callbacks are suitable for frontline authority with limits and logging.

bank.question: In which situation is the Banking Mohtasib Pakistan the most appropriate next step for the customer?
options: A mobile network keeps dropping calls and the operator has not fixed it
A customer remains dissatisfied after receiving her bank's final reply to a fee complaint
A customer has just noticed an incorrect charge on her bank account and has not yet told the bank
A life insurance claim has been declined after review by the insurer
bank.explanation: The Banking Mohtasib handles banking complaints, generally once the bank's own process has been used. A customer who has not yet complained should first go to the bank. Telecom issues go to the operator and then PTA; insurance complaints go to the Federal Insurance Ombudsman.

bank.question: A bank's quarterly complaint report to the board shows only the number of complaints received and the share closed within the target time. What important information is missing?
options: Root causes, trends by product and channel, repeat complaints and outcomes
The names and branches of the staff members involved in handling each complaint
Complaint numbers of competitor banks
A list of customers who complained most often
bank.explanation: Boards and regulators expect complaints to be analysed for causes, trends and outcomes so systemic issues are fixed. Counts and closure times alone cannot show what is going wrong. Naming staff or customers is inappropriate, and competitor numbers do not explain internal causes.

bank.question: A pilot of a new queue-management system runs in 10 branches. Their top-two-box CSAT rises 8 points over the quarter. Ten similar control branches without the system rise 5 points in the same period. What is the best estimate of the system's effect?
options: 8 points, as measured in the pilot
13 points, combining both increases
About 3 points, the difference from the control branches
Zero, because the control branches also improved
bank.explanation: The control group shows that about 5 points of improvement happened anyway. The pilot's extra 3 points is the best estimate of its effect, to be confirmed with more data. Claiming 8 ignores the control; zero ignores the extra gain.

bank.question: A contact centre handles 2.4 million calls a year; 15% are PIN-reset requests. App-based PIN reset is expected to remove 60% of those calls. Cost per call is PKR 90. The feature costs PKR 25 million one-off plus PKR 5 million a year to run. What is the approximate payback period?
options: About 1.3 years
About 1.7 years
About 2.6 years
About 0.8 years
bank.explanation: 2.4 million × 15% = 360,000 calls; × 60% = 216,000 fewer calls; × PKR 90 = PKR 19.44 million a year. Net of running costs: 19.44 − 5 = PKR 14.44 million. Payback = 25 ÷ 14.44 ≈ 1.7 years. 1.3 years ignores the running cost.

bank.question: Which of the following is the clearest sign that an organisation's CX effort has become theatre?
options: A CX forum that assigns owners and deadlines to the top five root causes
Frontline staff sharing one customer comment in each weekly huddle
A pilot with a control group to test a new onboarding call
A monthly dashboard reviewed by leaders with no decisions or actions recorded
bank.explanation: Reviewing scores without deciding anything is activity without change. Assigning owners to root causes, using customer comments in huddles and testing changes with controls are signs of real CX practice.

bank.question: A new CX strategy must name four priority journeys out of twenty. What is the best basis for choosing them?
options: Value at stake (customers, revenue, risk) combined with today's customer pain
The journeys that are easiest and cheapest to fix, so the programme shows quick results
The journeys owned by the most senior executives
The journeys with the most attractive digital design opportunities
bank.explanation: Priorities should balance value at stake and pain today, so effort goes where it matters most to customers and the business. Ease of fixing helps sequence quick wins but should not set the strategy alone; seniority and design appeal are not customer-based criteria.

bank.question: Asma Rehman joins a general insurer as head of CX with a 90-day mandate to show progress. Claims complaints are high and there is no CX governance. Which plan is strongest?
options: Launch NPS across every touchpoint immediately and link all staff bonuses to it from the first quarter
Begin by selecting and buying a large CX technology platform, then design the programme around its features
Pick two or three journeys from evidence, set up a forum with owners and deliver measured quick wins
Run a customer-service week with branding and train all staff in courtesy so that results show quickly
bank.explanation: Evidence-based priorities, governance with clear owners, quick wins and a measurement plan build credibility and real change. Linking bonuses to new, untested NPS invites gaming; leading with a technology purchase puts tools before problems; a branding week with courtesy training is theatre that ignores claims process causes.
